sections.heading: The stores sell belonging, not just books
paragraphs: Romance bookstores typically offer a different experience than a general shop. Customers get a judgment free zone, recommendations across a diverse range of subgenres, and a room full of people who read what they read. Many shops double as community hubs, with book clubs, writing workshops, and craft nights.

That is why the format survives online competition that was supposed to kill it. A website can ship a book cheaper. It cannot host the club, the workshop, or the feeling of being among your people. The store is the community with a cash register, not the other way around.

sections.heading: What niche retailers and creators can copy
paragraphs: The romance boom is a case study in audience first retail, and the moves translate well beyond books:
bullets: Pick one passionate audience and serve its full depth instead of stocking a shallow version of everything
Build where the community already gathers online, and make the physical space the place that community meets in person
Program the calendar, not just the shelves: clubs, workshops, and nights that give people a reason to return weekly
Let the audience see itself in the shop, from the name on the door to the sections on the wall

sections.heading: Print is not dead, unfocused print is
paragraphs: For years the story was that online shopping and social media would finish independent bookstores. The Hustle notes the twist: those very forces drove this resurgence. Social media built the audience, and the audience wanted a physical home.

The lesson is not that every niche gets a bookstore. It is that a defined community with real enthusiasm will support a focused business built for it, and will often prefer it to a giant general store that treats its passion as a back corner.

sources.title: The Hustle: Love and print is not dead (October 22, 2026)
The New School Free Press: The Ripped Bodice and writing romance (February 12, 2024)

title: AI Found Two Critical Flaws in the Code Behind 70 Percent of Websites
excerpt: PHP powers about 70 percent of websites, and two critical flaws rated 9.2 out of 10 sat in it for about a decade. AI models helped researchers find them, patches are out, and the NSA says anyone who cannot patch should take systems offline.
seoDescription: Two PHP flaws rated 9.2 of 10 put about 70 percent of websites at risk, and AI helped find them. What site owners should do this week.

image.alt: A collage of public posts from OpenAI, NSA Cyber, and The PHP Foundation warning about two critical PHP vulnerabilities rated CVSS 9.2, with a list of gaming and community sites taken down or put in maintenance
image.subject: PHP critical vulnerability warnings from OpenAI, NSA, and The PHP Foundation
image.credit: Image: PHP vulnerability posts collage via X and The Rundown AI. Story source: The Rundown AI, October 22, 2026

sections.heading: The patch everyone is scrambling to install
paragraphs: PHP, the programming language behind about 70 percent of websites, just pushed patches for two critical flaws found with help from OpenAI GPT 5.6 Sol. The Rundown reports OpenAI worked alongside the PHP maintainers for two months, and calls the find one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.

Morning Brew adds the scale of the response. The PHP Foundation rated both flaws at CVSS 9.2 out of 10, the fix took more than 10,000 lines of code, and the National Security Agency urged anyone who cannot patch right away to pull systems offline.

sections.heading: How the flaws were found
paragraphs: Security firm Calif found the first bug on August 1 using GPT 5.6 Sol. Wiz, the Google owned security firm, separately caught both flaws weeks later using Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. Multiple teams using AI found the same decade old bugs independently, which says something about how thoroughly models can now read old code.

Morning Brew reports the bug had actually been flagged years ago, but it was ranked low priority because it was deemed too complicated for a human hacker to untangle by hand. AI changed that math. What once took too long to exploit can now be worked out in hours or seconds, so the defenders had to move first.

sections.heading: What an attacker could do with them
paragraphs: The flaws let hackers hijack servers with no login at all. The NSA warning, quoted in the coverage, says these vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to a server file system or database. Morning Brew lists what that means in practice:
bullets: Alter a website content or appearance without the owner knowing
Run their own code on the server that hosts the site
Steal data stored on that server, including customer records

sections.heading: Governments took sites offline rather than wait
paragraphs: The response shows how seriously officials took it. Governments in Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands pulled websites offline, and Cloudflare said it was seeing early attacks emerging. Gaming and community services listed in the coverage went down or into maintenance, and 4chan went temporarily read only while awaiting the urgent PHP update.

Wiz cofounder Ami Luttwak, quoted by Morning Brew, called it the most severe AI vulnerability that was ever found. OpenAI says it has more major security finds like this still waiting to be disclosed, and describes the work as its Patch the Planet initiative, a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers preparing fixes ahead of disclosure.

sections.heading: What to do if you own a website
paragraphs: Basically every WordPress site runs on PHP, and WordPress powers a huge share of small business sites, portfolios, and stores. If that is you, this is a this week task, not a someday task:
bullets: Ask your host or developer which PHP version your site runs and whether the patch is applied
Update WordPress, themes, and plugins, and confirm your backups are current before you update
If your host cannot patch promptly, ask about taking the site offline briefly rather than leaving it exposed
Turn on automatic updates where your setup allows it, so the next urgent patch is not waiting on you

sections.heading: The deeper lesson about old code
paragraphs: The uncomfortable takeaway is that code written before AI is more fragile than anyone assumed. Bugs that were safe only because they were hard to find are not safe anymore, because finding them just got cheap. The same models that create the risk are also the best tool defenders have, which is why OpenAI framed this as a race the good side won this time.
For site owners, the practical version is simple. Maintenance is no longer invisible background work you can skip. It is part of what keeps the business open.

sources.title: The Rundown AI: AI finds a security hole in 70 percent of the web (October 22, 2026)

title: Claude Duet Works on Its Own Cloud Computer While Your Devices Are Off
excerpt: Anthropic launched Claude Duet, a proactive agent app built on Opus 5.5 that sends a morning brief, checks connected apps every few hours, and works on its own cloud computer even when your phone and laptop are off.
seoDescription: Claude Duet is a proactive agent that works while your devices are off. What it does, what it must ask before doing, and the limit to watch.

image.alt: Three phone screens showing the Claude Duet app preparing a location opening checklist, rebuilding a pitch deck, and drafting partner meeting prep, with a Link payment approval card
image.subject: Claude Duet app screens showing proactive agent work
image.credit: Image: Claude Duet app screens via Anthropic and The Rundown AI. Story source: The Neuron, October 22, 2026

sections.heading: An agent that checks in so you do not have to
paragraphs: Anthropic has launched Claude Duet, a standalone app where Claude acts as a proactive agent instead of waiting for your next prompt. The Neuron reports that Duet sends you a morning brief, checks your connected apps every few hours, and messages you only when something actually needs you.

Duet is a research preview for Pro and Max subscribers in the United States, rolling out by waitlist. It is built around Claude Opus 5.5, it counts against your normal Claude usage limits, and it carries over your Claude memory, skills, and connected apps. Anthropic lists more than 6,000 connectors, including QuickBooks, Stripe, Gusto, Docusign, HubSpot, and Shopify.

sections.heading: It runs on its own computer, not yours
paragraphs: The detail that changes the offer is where Duet lives. It runs on its own virtual machine, a small cloud computer with a browser, so it keeps working when your phone is in your pocket and your laptop is closed. The Rundown gives the shape of the work: morning briefs, calendar tracking, and booking meetings, handled in the background.

That is a real shift. A chatbot waits inside a window you open. Duet is closer to a staff member with a desk of its own, checking the inbox and the calendar on a schedule and bringing you the short list.

sections.heading: The brakes are the product
paragraphs: An agent that acts while you are not looking raises one obvious question: what stops it from doing something costly or embarrassing? Anthropic answer is a stack of brakes, and The Neuron lists them plainly:
bullets: Duet shows exactly what it is about to do and waits for your approval before sending a message, making a payment, signing a document, or deleting anything
Trading securities and moving money between accounts are off limits, even with your approval
Credentials follow the Managed Agents design, so Duet never sees your passwords or tokens and has nothing to leak
A classifier blocks sharing the most sensitive information, like card numbers and government IDs, and health and finance details go out only when you say so

sections.heading: It can pay, within the approval screen
paragraphs: On payments, Duet can use Link, the Stripe wallet, with a one time virtual card, and Shop Pay. The Rundown notes the same guardrail: deletion, payment, signature, and outgoing messages all need your sign off first. An AI can now buy things for you, which makes reading the approval screen a genuine job skill.

Anthropic is also candid about the weak spots. Duet can misread a thread or misjudge urgency, it is weaker at personal errands than at work tasks, and it cannot yet show you its browser while it works.

sections.heading: The number that decides whether it lasts
paragraphs: The Neuron names the metric that matters: the ping threshold. Ping too often and Duet becomes the coworker you mute. Ping too rarely and you miss the showing, the deadline, or the client who needed an answer today. Urgency judgment is the weak spot Anthropic itself admits to.

There is a second cost. Background checks and big tasks count against your usage limits, so the assistant that never sleeps also spends your quota while you do. Track two numbers in the first month: how many pings were worth attention, and how much usage the background work consumed.

sections.heading: What this means for anyone who directs work from a phone
paragraphs: Duet is the clearest sign yet that the job is moving from doing tasks to directing and approving them. The valuable human is no longer the fastest typist. It is the person who sets the brief and reads an approval screen with care.

Start narrow if you get access. Give it one job with a clear finish line, like a morning brief, and judge it on whether its interruptions earn their place. Widen the brief only after the pings prove themselves.

sources.title: The Neuron: Claude Duet just launched (October 22, 2026)
The Rundown AI: Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet (October 22, 2026)

title: Williams Sonoma Grew by Selling to Businesses While Home Sales Stalled
excerpt: With home buying still slow, Williams Sonoma leaned into business customers. The Hustle reports its stock up more than 200 percent in three years, business revenue up 14.5 percent in the quarter, and contract revenue up 20 percent, with cruise ships, senior living, and student housing next.
seoDescription: Williams Sonoma business revenue rose 14.5 percent as home sales stalled. Contract work up 20 percent and the second buyer lesson for brands.

image.alt: A furnished cruise ship deck with a yellow armchair, a side table with a plant, and a floor lamp beside a white railing over the sea
image.subject: Furniture on a cruise ship deck
image.credit: Image: Cruise ship deck furniture illustration via The Hustle. Story source: The Hustle, October 21, 2026

sections.heading: A furniture business with too few home buyers
paragraphs: Home sales in 2026 are slightly higher than last year, but remain well below the long running average, as high prices and mortgage rates keep buyers sidelined. When people stop buying homes, they stop filling them, and home retailers feel it quickly. Value City Furniture liquidated.

Williams Sonoma Inc., the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm, went the other way. The Hustle reports its stock has risen by more than 200 percent over three years. Part of that is a customer base that analyst Neil Saunders of GlobalData describes as more insulated from economic stress. The other part is a second business hiding inside the first one.

sections.heading: The second buyer is a business
paragraphs: Alongside selling to households, the company leaned into selling to businesses that furnish spaces on a schedule rather than on a whim. Saunders notes that selling to businesses is different, but not so different that it becomes inefficient, so the company can fish in both pools and balance its revenue.
The numbers from the company 2026 second quarter earnings call, as reported by The Hustle, show the second pool growing faster:
bullets: Business to business revenue increased 14.5 percent in the quarter
Contract revenue grew 20 percent, and trade revenue grew 12 percent, per finance chief Jeff Howie
Contract revenue accounted for 36 percent of the business to business segment

sections.heading: Where the business orders are coming from
paragraphs: The company named cruise ships, senior living, and student housing as markets it is expanding into, and the completed projects show the range: Virgin Hotels in New York City, Signature Aviation Miami Executive Airport here in Florida, the University of Texas at Austin Hardin House, and the Carneros Inn in Napa.

There is a logic to the list. Cruise ships, dormitories, and care homes get refreshed far more often than a family living room, because wear is constant and appearance is part of what their customers pay for. A business buyer is not decorating once. It is maintaining a standard, on a cycle, with a budget for it.

sections.heading: It is not the only brand fishing in both pools
paragraphs: Saunders points out that IKEA runs a large business operation for office furnishings and Amazon runs a huge one generating billions. The shared pattern is a focus on what business buyers need: volume, durability, repeatable ordering, and accountability.

There is a risk. Styles that appear in every hotel and dorm can start to feel common, which dulls the premium feel sold to households. The company is betting most guests and students will never notice, and that steady contract revenue is worth more than the lost mystique.

sections.heading: The lesson for smaller brands is direct
paragraphs: Most small brands and service businesses sell to one buyer and stop. The Williams Sonoma move is to ask a simple question when that buyer slows down: who else already needs this same skill or product, on a schedule, with a budget?
bullets: A slow consumer market does not mean demand vanished, it may have moved to a different buyer
Business buyers purchase on cycles, which makes revenue easier to plan around
The offer usually needs adjusting, not rebuilding, because the craft underneath stays the same
One contract customer can be worth a season of one time household sales

sections.heading: Coverage businesses can run the same play
paragraphs: The parallel for a Florida creative business is close. A couple books a wedding once. A venue, festival, or hotel group books coverage again and again, on dates known months ahead. It is the same craft pointed at a buyer with a calendar and a budget.

Williams Sonoma did not abandon home buyers. It built a second pool to fish in while the first one was quiet. When your main market stalls, the useful question is rarely how to shout louder at it. It is who else is already buying what you make.

sources.title: The Hustle: A home brand sets sail, Williams Sonoma furnished a comeback without homebuyers (October 21, 2026)

title: She Makes About 13,000 Dollars a Month Moving Strangers, and Trust Is the Product
excerpt: Hannah Crawford started Han with a Van in April 2025 with Facebook posts and rented vans. The Hustle Blower and SWNS report about 10,000 pounds a month in turnover, a network of about 20 movers across the UK, and a goal of 100 moves a month.
seoDescription: Han with a Van grew to about 13,000 dollars a month by selling trust to women moving home. The niche, the rented van start, and the network model.

image.alt: Hannah Crawford smiling in the driver seat of her moving van, photographed through the open passenger window
image.subject: Hannah Crawford of Han with a Van in her van
image.credit: Image: Hannah Crawford photo by Lauren James Photography via SWNS. Story sources: The Hustle Blower and SWNS, October 2026

sections.heading: The problem was never moving furniture
paragraphs: In April 2025, Hannah Crawford, a 29 year old theater producer in London, started a side hustle helping people move. Instead of marketing herself as one more affordable mover, she aimed at a problem competitors were not talking about. Moving means inviting strangers into your home and trusting them on a stressful day.

For women moving alone or leaving difficult relationships, that trust question can decide who gets hired. Hannah posted in Facebook groups offering a move built to feel comfortable and reassuring, aimed at women and LGBTQ customers. When someone booked, she rented a van and did the job herself.

sections.heading: Customers told her exactly why it worked
paragraphs: Women messaged her with stories about earlier moves: careless service and broken belongings. One described a mover who, after learning where she lived, started sending unwanted messages. That story explains the whole business.

A typical moving company sells transportation and labor, and Hannah sells the same things. What she added was a promise about how the customer would feel. She was not competing on who could carry a sofa fastest, but on who a customer felt comfortable inviting through the front door. That made her offer easy to recommend in seconds.

sections.heading: Six day weeks, then one video changed the scale
paragraphs: By July 2025, Hannah says she was booked six days a week. People already paid movers. She had given one group a stronger reason to choose her.

In June 2026 she posted an Instagram video about helping a woman move after a breakup, and it spread widely. SWNS reports she gained 8,300 followers in two weeks. By September demand passed what one person could carry, so she built a network of about 20 movers across the UK. The business reports about 10,000 pounds a month in turnover, roughly 13,000 dollars. Her goal of 100 moves and 50,000 pounds a month is a target, not a result, and turnover is revenue before costs come out.

sections.heading: The model underneath the story
paragraphs: SWNS describes how a job runs now. A customer asks for a quote based on the size and distance of the move. Once agreed, the job goes onto a board where an available mover can accept it. The quote splits into a service fee, van equipment and insurance, and travel and fuel beyond 20 miles.

That structure is the real transition. At the start, her income depended on how many sofas she could personally carry. Now her job is demand, pricing, finding reliable movers, and protecting the promised experience. An illustrative model in The Hustle Blower, 20 moves at 500 pounds with about 300 pounds of direct costs each, leaves roughly 4,000 pounds before overhead and taxes. Positioning wins the customer. Operations decide whether the money survives.

sections.heading: Steal the positioning, not the van
paragraphs: The opportunity is not starting a moving company. It is applying her sequence to any ordinary service people already pay for, from cleaning and photography to event coverage.
bullets: Pick a service with existing demand
Find the group that dislikes the normal buying experience, and learn the exact frustration in their words
Build the offer around removing that one frustration, and say it plainly
Test with community posts and rented or borrowed capacity before buying equipment
Write delivery standards down before others represent the business

sections.heading: Trust is a promise operations must keep
paragraphs: Scaling a trust based offer is the hard part. Finding 20 people who can move furniture is one thing. Finding 20 who communicate well, arrive on time, and handle belongings carefully is another, and one bad job can damage the reputation the niche was built on.

Florida service businesses should recognize the shape of this. Customers here also book strangers into their homes and events. The business that names the fear everyone else ignores, then builds a process that removes it every time, does not need to be the cheapest option in town.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: Her Unusual Moving Business Makes 13K a Month (October 21, 2026)
SWNS: I make 13K a month helping women move after breakups (October 2026)

title: Two Creator Reviews Turned an 8,500 Dollar Bag Idea Into 1.7 Million in Sales
excerpt: Makeup artist Alexandra Rutkay started citymouse with about 8,500 dollars after her purse could not fit her son essentials. The Hustle Blower reports more than 1.7 million dollars in total sales and 20,000 customers, after two reviews sold 500 bags in three days.
seoDescription: citymouse passed 1.7 million dollars in sales from an 8,500 dollar start after two creator reviews sold 500 bags in 3 days. The distribution lesson.

image.alt: A model wearing the sky blue citymouse Park crossbody bag with a wide branded strap, photographed against a white background
image.subject: citymouse Park crossbody bag product photo
image.credit: Image: citymouse Park bag product photo via citymouse. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 20, 2026

sections.heading: A gap between two products became one bag
paragraphs: Alexandra Rutkay was getting ready for dinner with her husband and son when she hit a familiar problem. Her nice purse could not fit her son sippy cup, diapers, and wipes, and she did not want to carry an enormous diaper bag to dinner. So she designed something in between: a small, stylish crossbody bag that holds parenting essentials without looking like baby gear. She called it citymouse.

Alexandra was not a handbag designer. She was a New York makeup artist working long hours on film and television sets, and she started with about 8,500 dollars. The bag she sketched combined a drink holder, diaper storage, card slots, a changing pad, and interchangeable straps. A few years later, The Hustle Blower reports, the company had passed 1.7 million dollars in sales and 20,000 customers.

sections.heading: The first 500 bags took more than six months
paragraphs: This was not an overnight success. Alexandra shared the product on TikTok, launched with preorders that helped fund production, and kept her regular job while the business grew slowly. Her first 500 bags took more than six months to sell.

During that slow stretch she experimented with new colors and straps and improved the product while a small audience formed. A useful product does not find its own customers. Someone still has to put it in front of them.

sections.heading: Two reviews did what six months could not
paragraphs: In 2024, while Alexandra was working long days on a movie set, two positive reviews of the bags gained traction on TikTok and Instagram. Within three days the company sold out more than 500 bags, the same number that had taken half a year the first time. She quickly ordered another 1,000 bags from her manufacturer.

The product had not changed. The audience had. Earlier reporting cited by The Hustle Blower says referrals eventually accounted for roughly 90 percent of the business at that stage. A creator showing how much fits inside the bag persuades in a way an advertisement cannot, because the demonstration is the proof.

sections.heading: How she kept the attention working
paragraphs: citymouse generated about 135,000 dollars in sales in 2023, and what followed was a mix, not a miracle. The brand kept posting its own content, spent about 25,000 dollars on Facebook ads in 2024, and joined TikTok Shop in spring 2024, where a three day stretch brought roughly 50,000 dollars in sales because viewers could buy without leaving the platform.

By October 2026 the reported total passed 1.7 million dollars across the website, TikTok Shop, and wholesale. Outside reviews created the spike, and owned content, paid ads, and new channels turned it into a business.

sections.heading: The copyable play for any small product
paragraphs: You do not need your own large following to test this. You need a product whose benefit is obvious in seconds, and people whose audiences already have the problem it solves.
bullets: List 20 to 30 small creators who already review products like yours, and study whether their viewers ask buying questions
Offer a sample and an honest review, with any payment or commission disclosed properly
Ask for a real demonstration on a real day, not a script full of marketing claims
Track which creators bring profitable orders with unique links or codes, then find more who resemble the winners

sections.heading: Attention exposes weak operations fast
paragraphs: The rush nearly broke the business. Orders were packed in the living room, inventory was counted by hand, and repeated sellouts risked the momentum. The original rubber logos peeled off the nylon, so Alexandra switched to stitched logos. Competitors arrived, and her husband eventually left his career to run operations full time.
Distribution made the business take off, and operations let it survive taking off. Build the creator list before the big inventory order, and the stock plan before the creator posts.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: She Sold 1.7M Fixing One Annoyance (October 20, 2026)
citymouse: The Park Bag crossbody diaper bag

title: A Factory AI Startup Just Debuted at a 1.5 Billion Dollar Valuation
excerpt: Former OpenAI research chief Bob McGrew came out of stealth with Arda, which plans factory assembly lines from design files. The Rundown reports a 160 million dollar Series A, a 1.5 billion dollar valuation, and a first customer, Anduril, cutting basic assembly instructions from 10 hours to 15 minutes.
seoDescription: Arda debuted at a 1.5 billion dollar valuation with AI that plans factory lines. Anduril cut assembly instructions from 10 hours to 15 minutes.

image.alt: An Arda graphic showing its four step factory planning process, from translating designs into a manufacturing process to reconfiguring the factory as conditions change
image.subject: Arda factory planning process graphic
image.credit: Image: Arda process graphic via The Rundown AI. Story source: The Rundown AI, October 21, 2026

sections.heading: The pitch is Claude for factory engineers
paragraphs: Former OpenAI Chief Research Officer Bob McGrew just came out of stealth with Arda, a startup building AI that helps factories set up assembly lines for new products far faster. The Rundown reports that Arda launches at a 1.5 billion dollar valuation after a 160 million dollar Series A round, which is a remarkable price for a company most people had never heard of a week ago.

McGrew pitched Arda as doing for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers. The software reads design files and plans the build: operations, tools, stations, and the instructions a line needs to make a new product.

sections.heading: Why changing a factory line is so expensive
paragraphs: The comparison McGrew draws is with factories in Asia, where big crews can relearn a new design in about a day. An automated line in the United States moves slower. Reprogramming a single automated station can cost nearly 1 million dollars, and every new product can mean weeks of planning before the first unit rolls off.

That gap is the whole business. A factory that switches products quickly can take jobs competitors decline, and wastes less equipment time sitting idle. Speed of change, not speed of production, is the prize.

sections.heading: The first customer reports a dramatic time cut
paragraphs: Defense firm Anduril is Arda first customer, and its report is the number that will sell the next ten deals. Basic assembly instructions that once took 10 hours now take 15 minutes, and Anduril says it would be behind without the technology. Treat that as a customer claim in a launch story, not a measured study, but even a fraction of that gain would pay for a lot of software.

McGrew wants to go further. The next step is robots on the line, reprogrammed by Arda agents in days instead of weeks. His stated goal is a fully automated version of Shenzhen in West Texas, which tells you the ambition is not a planning tool. It is a new way to run a factory.

sections.heading: The exodus from the frontier labs continues
paragraphs: McGrew joins Mira Murati, Ilya Sutskever, and other senior OpenAI departures now running billion dollar startups of their own. Arda is the rare one building for physical production instead of building another frontier model, and that choice is part of the story investors are buying.

The timing helps too. The Rundown notes that Jeff Bezos project Prometheus raised 12 billion dollars for an artificial general engineer focused on designing physical products. Serious money now believes the next big AI market is not only words and images. It is things you can hold.

sections.heading: What builders outside factories should take from this
paragraphs: The pattern is the same one winning in creative work. The valuable tool is not the one that generates the most. It is the one that shortens the distance between a finished design and a finished product, inside a workflow that already costs real money when it moves slowly.
bullets: Find the step where a skilled person spends hours translating one format into another
Measure the current time honestly, the way Anduril 10 hours to 15 minutes claim does
Sell the recovered time and the jobs it unlocks, not the model behind the tool
Start with one customer whose result can carry the next round of sales

sections.heading: Planning is becoming the product
paragraphs: Factories spent a century getting better at making the same thing. The new contest is getting better at making the next thing, and AI that plans the changeover attacks exactly that weakness. Whether Arda holds its valuation is a question for its investors.

For everyone else, the signal is simpler. In field after field, the plan itself is turning into software work. People who document their process clearly will hand that work to AI first, and move first when the market changes.

sources.title: The Rundown AI: Ex OpenAI research chief Arda debuts at 1.5B (October 21, 2026)

title: Shared Meta Muse Chats Were Findable Without the Link
excerpt: Claroc found more than 6,800 shared Meta Muse chat addresses in public web records, and Meta paused the sharing feature while it investigates. The Neuron reports the chat title sat inside the address itself, and some shared pages held loan applications, revenue reviews, and staff calendars.
seoDescription: More than 6,800 shared Meta Muse chats were findable in public DNS records, Claroc found. Why a share link is a public page and what to share instead.

image.alt: A Neuron illustration of a worried cat at a laptop beside search results for shared Muse chats, an open padlock, and papers labeled Public Records
image.subject: Meta Muse shared chats publicly findable illustration
image.credit: Image: Illustration via The Neuron. Story source: The Neuron, October 21, 2026

sections.heading: Sharing a chat publishes a page
paragraphs: Security firm Claroc says anyone could find chats shared from Meta Muse app without being sent the link. The Neuron reports Claroc found more than 6,800 share addresses in public internet records, and The Verge reports Meta paused Muse sharing while it investigates.

Tap share in Muse and the chat becomes a web page that opens for anyone who has the link, with no login needed. That openness is the feature, because it is how a coworker or a client reads the chat. It is also the risk, because a shared link is not private once the page exists.

sections.heading: The chat title was printed inside the address
paragraphs: The twist is how Muse built each address. The page address combined the chat title with a random code, so a chat about a budget review carried that topic in readable words inside the link itself. The random code was supposed to make the address hard to guess.

It did not stay secret. Every time a browser opens a page, it looks the address up in DNS, the system that turns web addresses into server locations. Services called passive DNS log those lookups and let people search them. Claroc searched one and the chat titles came back readable, like a table of contents. The full address, code included, was logged the first time anyone opened the page.

sections.heading: What strangers could open and read
paragraphs: Claroc opened a few hundred of the pages without logging in. Most were harmless, like small business sites and event calendars. A minority were the kind of thing nobody means to publish:
bullets: Prep notes for a confidential call with a frontier AI lab, including an internal contact and a meeting time
An internal revenue review at a marketing company, marked for its chief executive
A small business loan application with the amount requested
A staff vacation calendar covering a full year and listing dozens of employees

sections.heading: The app is big, and the caveats matter
paragraphs: Muse is not small. Sensor Tower data cited by The Neuron shows the app passed 10.9 million downloads in its first 40 days, and Meta put 39 percent of its October advertising spend behind it. An app collecting that much trust that fast collects sensitive chats too.

Keep the caveats in view. Claroc sells software that spots risky AI sharing, so it has a stake in this story. Its search covered one service, one address pattern, and a short window, and it reports no evidence anyone misused the pages, which were public because their owners shared them. Claroc reported the issue to Meta on October 8, and still spotted 27 new share addresses on the day it last checked.

sections.heading: A safer way to share AI work
paragraphs: Treat every share link in every AI app as a public web page, because that is what it is. Before you send one, read the chat the way a stranger would, and ask what it reveals about a client, a price, a plan, or a person who never agreed to be in it.
bullets: Never share a chat that holds client names, prices, contracts, or unreleased plans
Copy the useful part into a document you control, and share that document instead
Give the copy a plain title that reveals nothing about the client or the deal
Delete shared chats you no longer need, and assume old links still work until you check

sections.heading: The lesson travels beyond one app
paragraphs: Nothing here required a hacker to break in. The door was the share button, and the address on the door was written in plain language. Creators now do real client work inside AI chats every day, which makes chat hygiene part of client trust.
The fix is boring and fast. Share less, copy out only what the other person needs, and keep the working chat private.

sources.title: The Neuron: Meta Muse made shared chats searchable (October 21, 2026)

title: Mercury 3 Drafts Answers All at Once and It Is Very Fast
excerpt: Inception launched Mercury 3, a diffusion language model that drafts many words at once instead of one at a time. The Rundown reports output above 1,000 tokens a second and pricing at 0.20 and 0.70 dollars per million tokens, and The Neuron test of eight runs cost about four cents in total.
seoDescription: Mercury 3 diffusion model claims 1,000 plus tokens a second at 0.20 and 0.70 dollars per million tokens. The four cent test kit any creator can copy.

image.alt: An Inception chart titled Model Quality versus Model Size showing five Mercury generations from M1 mini to M3, with M3 marked about 8 times faster than GPT 6 Luna in October 2026
image.subject: Mercury generations speed chart
image.credit: Image: Inception Mercury chart via The Rundown AI. Story source: The Rundown AI, October 20, 2026

sections.heading: A different way to write, not just a faster chip
paragraphs: Most language models write one token at a time, left to right, like a person typing without ever deleting. Inception Mercury 3 works differently. It is a diffusion model, which drafts many words at once and then refines them, more like an editor revising a whole draft than a typist composing a sentence. The Rundown reports that this approach produces output above 1,000 tokens a second.

Inception says Mercury 3 matches or beats GPT 6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on its own numbers while running four to eight times faster, and that it is 40 times the size of Mercury 1 while holding the same speed. Pricing is 0.20 dollars per million input tokens and 0.70 dollars per million output tokens. Those quality claims are the company own, and both newsletters treat them that way.

sections.heading: Where speed actually changes the product
paragraphs: Mercury will not replace the frontier models people use for hard reasoning, and Inception is not pretending otherwise. Speed wins a different set of jobs, the ones where any lag is visible to a user:
bullets: Live tutors that have to answer while a student is still paying attention
Voice customer support, where a pause feels like a failure
Web browsing agents that take many small steps in a row
Any app where a person waits on screen while the model thinks

sections.heading: One tester ran eight trials for about four cents
paragraphs: The Neuron adds the most practical part of the story. Corey Noles ran Mercury 3 through eight API runs, including a constrained science fiction story, a coffee shop math problem, an explain it three ways prompt, a single file dungeon crawler game, a made up NASA mission designed to catch invented facts, and a classic logic puzzle. The whole bill came to about four cents.

The results were mixed in instructive ways. The math was essentially right, including a 900 dollar daily gross profit figure, and it questioned the problem assumptions. The game code passed a syntax check and 2,000 randomized map checks with no failures. The story ran about 274 words against a 250 word limit, and on the fake NASA mission it flagged the fabrication but added an unrelated error of its own. Fast and cheap did not mean careless, and it did not mean flawless either.

sections.heading: Steal the test kit for your own work
paragraphs: The method matters more than the model. Corey advice, as reported by The Neuron, is to test any new model on tasks from your actual work instead of trusting launch charts: one task with strict limits, one math word problem, one coding or building request, and one question built on a fake premise to see whether it invents facts.

Then grade the misses instead of the vibes. Count the words when a limit was set. Check the arithmetic by hand. Open the code and run it. A model that fails your own test in a way you can see is giving you more information than a benchmark chart from the company selling it.

sections.heading: Why creators should care about a speed race
paragraphs: The Rundown notes that OpenAI is pushing speed too, with a Cerebras partnership and an Ultrafast tier for GPT 6 Astra reaching as high as 300 tokens a second. When answers arrive almost instantly and cost almost nothing, the bottleneck in creative work moves. It stops being generation and becomes selection: which draft, which take, which idea is actually good.

That is good news for people with taste and bad news for people selling raw output by the hour. Try Mercury Chat or OpenRouter with the four cent test above, run it against the tools you already pay for, and let your own work decide. Speed is clearly the next battleground, and small teams that test early will know exactly where the new models fit before their competitors do.

sources.title: The Rundown AI: Inception Mercury 3 speeds past rivals (October 20, 2026)
The Neuron: Test a new AI model on your own work for about four cents (October 20, 2026)

title: An Anthropic Co Founder Says the Singularity Has Begun
excerpt: Jack Clark told the IMF and World Bank annual meetings that the singularity has now begun, The Rundown reports. He pointed to Humanity Last Exam scores rising from 8 percent to 67.7 percent, FrontierMath from 2 percent to 94 percent, and a model with United States GDP at 44 trillion dollars by 2030.
seoDescription: Jack Clark told the IMF the singularity has begun, citing exam scores from 8 to 67.7 percent and a 44 trillion dollar GDP model. What creators should make of it.

image.alt: An IMF presentation slide reading The singularity, when AI systems speed up the pace of overall scientific and technical progress in a way that is hard for humans to comprehend, beside Jack Clark speaking at a podium
image.subject: Jack Clark singularity IMF slide
image.credit: Image: IMF presentation still via The Rundown AI. Story source: The Rundown AI, October 20, 2026

sections.heading: He said it to the people who run the global economy
paragraphs: Anthropic has spent 2026 warning that AI is moving faster than anyone is ready for. Now one of its co founders has given the moment a name, in front of the most establishment audience imaginable. The Rundown reports that Jack Clark told economists and policymakers at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings that the singularity has now begun.

His definition, shown on his own slide, is plain: the point when AI systems speed up the pace of overall scientific and technical progress in a way that is hard for humans to comprehend. This was not a podcast hot take. It was a co founder of a leading AI lab saying it on the record to the institutions that manage money and policy for the whole world.

sections.heading: The score jumps he used as evidence
paragraphs: Clark pointed to test results that are hard to wave away, even allowing for the fact that benchmarks are an imperfect measure of real ability:
bullets: Scores on Humanity Last Exam, a set of expert level questions, rose from 8 percent to 67.7 percent since 2025
FrontierMath performance improved from 2 percent to 94 percent over the same period
One Anthropic model puts United States GDP at 44 trillion dollars by 2030 if AI spreads fast, a figure Clark admitted sounds outlandish
He predicted very disruptive job impacts alongside that growth, and said the world 10 million scientists may soon direct a billion virtual scientists

sections.heading: He also talked about a ceiling on intelligence
paragraphs: The most striking part may be what Clark said about limits. He told the audience that chief executive Dario Amodei has floated limits on AI ceiling of intelligence, and that he believes there is only a small number of years left to act on questions like that. He also urged nations to build labs and robots before they run short.

Read that carefully. A leader inside one of the top labs is publicly discussing whether the technology should have a cap, while his own company races to build more of it. Whether you find that reassuring or alarming, it tells you the people closest to the work no longer treat runaway progress as a distant thought experiment.

sections.heading: Why this matters outside the IMF room
paragraphs: Singularity talk used to live in science fiction and in fringe corners of the internet. When it is delivered at the IMF, it becomes planning input for governments and big employers. Budgets, training programs, and hiring plans get shaped by what leaders in that room believe is coming, whether or not the boldest version arrives on schedule.

For small studios and creators, the practical translation is less dramatic and more useful. Tools will keep getting better at the draft stage of almost every job: research, first cuts, captions, layouts, and code. The scarce skills move toward judgment, taste, client trust, and finishing work to a standard a person will sign their name to.

sections.heading: Hold the claim and the caution at the same time
paragraphs: Clark has every incentive to make his industry sound world changing, and exam scores are not the same thing as scientific discovery in the wild. A healthy reader keeps both facts in view. The claim is promotional, and the trend underneath it is real enough that finance ministers are being briefed on it.

The useful response is not panic and not dismissal. It is to build your work so that each new wave of capability makes you faster instead of obsolete: own the client relationship, own the final call on quality, and let the machines carry the volume. If Clark is even half right about the pace, that positioning is the safest seat in the room.

sources.title: The Rundown AI: Anthropic co founder says the singularity is underway (October 20, 2026)

title: He Made 400,000 Dollars in a Record Month Cleaning Dog Yards
excerpt: William Milliken co founded Swoop Scoop after a bad experience hiring a dog waste service for his own yard. The Hustle Blower reports more than 2,500 customers at a little over 110 dollars a month, a first month past 400,000 dollars in revenue, and a quarterly billing group 72 percent less likely to cancel.
seoDescription: Swoop Scoop passed 2,500 customers at about 110 dollars a month and a record month past 400,000 dollars. The 6 dollar lead, route density, and billing lesson.

image.alt: A smiling woman holding a small fluffy white dog outdoors beside the Swoop Scoop logo on a teal background
image.subject: Swoop Scoop customer holding dog
image.credit: Image: Swoop Scoop customer and dog photo via Swoop Scoop. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 20, 2026

sections.heading: It started with a pregnant wife and a bad service
paragraphs: In late 2020, William Milliken backyard was full of dog waste, his wife was pregnant, and the dog waste removal service she hired was inconsistent, hard to reach, and confusing on billing. William knew home service marketing, and his friend Levi wanted to start a company but had no specialized trade. They needed something simple and worth paying for again and again.

So Levi practiced in his own backyard by scattering rocks and timing how long it took to collect them. He did not own a dog. That test answered the key question: how many yards can one person clean in a day? In 2021, their first full year, Swoop Scoop reported more than 260,000 dollars in revenue and more than 300 recurring customers.

sections.heading: The winning ad was a bag of waste in the snow
paragraphs: Their first 15 to 20 customers came from door knocking, door hangers, veterinary contacts, and neighborhood groups. Then paid social ads took over, and one of the strongest creatives was disarmingly simple: a photo of a filled waste bag sitting in the snow. For a dog owner staring at a winter worth of surprises in the yard, the message needed no explanation.

William reported leads at about 6 to 7 dollars each, with roughly one in three or four leads becoming a customer. That implies an ad cost of about 18 to 28 dollars to acquire a customer who pays a little over 110 dollars a month on average. Those are historical figures, not a promise for a new market, and they leave out labor and other costs. Still, a boring service people keep buying makes a small acquisition cost valuable.

sections.heading: The real business is subscriptions and routes
paragraphs: A one time 25 dollar cleanup is a job. A customer paying every week, month after month, is a base you can build on. William reported that one technician could service about 125 to 150 recurring customers on tightly organized routes, around 25 to 35 yards a day. Geography is the hidden margin:
bullets: At 25 dollars a visit, a dense route finishing three visits an hour grosses about 75 dollars an hour before expenses
The same visit scattered across town, at 45 minutes per job, grosses about 33 dollars an hour
Five customers on one street can be worth more than five customers in five neighborhoods
In a 2026 interview William reported a first month past 400,000 dollars in company revenue, across multiple states and more than 2,500 customers

sections.heading: Quarterly billing customers canceled far less
paragraphs: The most useful detail may be about billing, not waste. William noticed customers paying quarterly were about 72 percent less likely to cancel than customers paying monthly, and nearly 40 percent of customers used quarterly or annual arrangements, sometimes with discounts. A monthly bill asks a customer to decide again every few weeks. A prepaid quarter quietly becomes part of the routine.

The caution matters: prepaid customers may simply be more committed, so this shows an association, not proof that billing alone caused the loyalty. Money collected upfront is not earned until visits are delivered. Even so, how you charge can matter almost as much as what you sell.

sections.heading: What a Florida service owner should copy
paragraphs: Start with one neighborhood, not a whole city. Get the first ten paying customers close together, learn your real travel and cleaning times, and expand into the next neighborhood only after the route makes sense. Turning down a distant customer can feel painful and still be the profitable call.

William and Levi did not invent a better service. They ran an ordinary one better: show up reliably, communicate clearly, and bill cleanly. In Florida, reliable and boring beats brilliant and flaky almost every time.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: He Made 400K Cleaning Dog Yards (October 20, 2026)
Swoop Scoop: Spokane Pooper Scooper Service

title: They Booked 50,000 Dollars Renting Wedding Cameras They Did Not Own
excerpt: Felipe Rochi and Rachel Calaj built a basic site for Pass the Cam before they owned a single camera. The Hustle Blower reports more than 50,000 dollars in business volume since May, from packages at 429, 699, and 899 dollars, after a first bride forced a 1,100 dollar shopping trip.
seoDescription: Pass the Cam passed 50,000 dollars renting wedding camcorders guests film on, at 429 to 899 dollars. The 1,100 dollar first camera and the logistics lesson.

image.alt: A bride in a white wedding dress putting on her shoe in a bright room with tall windows, captured in the soft candid style of a wedding home movie still
image.subject: Wedding camcorder home movie bride still
image.credit: Image: Wedding home movie still via TheWeddingCam, a wedding camcorder rental service. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 19, 2026

sections.heading: The first customer arrived before the camera did
paragraphs: In April 2026, Felipe Rochi was working in search engine optimization and Rachel Calaj was a contract school psychologist, and they were expecting their first baby. Felipe had already tried a remote jobs newsletter and a small pet product with no breakthrough. Then he noticed people renting camcorders to couples getting married, with guests doing the filming and a service turning the footage into a finished video.

He did the sensible thing first. He built a basic website, started posting short videos, and tested whether strangers wanted the offer before buying any gear. Then one Friday evening a message arrived: a bride whose videographer had canceled, with her wedding the following weekend. There was one problem. Felipe did not own a camcorder.

sections.heading: A 1,100 dollar shopping trip became proof
paragraphs: Felipe went shopping and spent about 1,100 dollars on a Sony 4K camcorder, a memory card, and a warranty. He packed it, shipped it, and when the footage came back he edited the video himself because hiring an editor was not in the budget. The customer was happy, and before May ended two more clients had booked.

Then the stakes changed. In early June Felipe lost one of his jobs, the day before their baby shower, and Rachel contract had ended in May. A side experiment suddenly had to carry real weight. The couple reported more than 50,000 dollars in business volume since May, and their stated goal is 100 clients by the end of 2026. Business volume is not profit, and the story is careful about that difference.

sections.heading: Guests are not a downgrade, they are the feature
paragraphs: A bride does not wake up wanting a camcorder shipped to her house. She wants a wedding video without paying thousands for a full production crew, and without begging friends to send phone clips afterward. Pass the Cam sits in the gap between those two options: a structured way for guests to capture the terrible dancing, the unfiltered speeches, and the moments a professional crew would never think to film.
The packages show the model plainly:
bullets: Starter at 429 dollars, a middle tier at 699 dollars, and Deluxe at 899 dollars
Higher tiers change the equipment, accessories, and finished video length
The same camera can be rented again and again, so one purchase becomes a repeating asset
At an illustrative 699 dollars with assumed costs, the first camera cost could be recovered after roughly three bookings, before marketing and overhead

sections.heading: The real business is logistics, not cameras
paragraphs: A camera booked for a Saturday wedding has to ship early, get used, come back, get inspected, get recharged, and go out again. A camera sitting in a delivery truck earns nothing, one late return can hurt the next couple, and one damaged memory card can threaten footage that can never be shot again. You cannot ask a couple to move their wedding to Tuesday.

That is why this is a logistics business wearing a wedding dress. Backup equipment, tracking, delivery buffers, clear return instructions, and an editing process that survives peak season matter more than a clever name. Copying the website and buying one camcorder is the easy part. Delivering the promise every time is the business.

sections.heading: What Florida creators should steal from this
paragraphs: Felipe reversed the usual order: audience first, inventory second. He posted the concept, got a paying customer, and only then spent the 1,100 dollars. Every finished wedding can also become the next advertisement, with the couple permission, because the product itself produces emotional proof.

For Florida videographers, the lesson is not to abandon professional work. It is to notice customers who were never going to buy it. A simpler, cheaper offer can serve a different buyer without lowering the premium price. Sometimes removing the professional from part of the process is not a downgrade. Sometimes it is the whole product.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: This Boring Rental Idea Made 50K Plus (October 19, 2026)

title: AI Hackers Left Their Own Dashboards Wide Open
excerpt: NorForge found more than 20 open control panels for Cairn, an AI hacking tool criminals used against real online stores. The Neuron and The Rundown report about 1,100 projects in one cluster, a roughly 10 percent success estimate, and break ins that cost about 50 dollars in model fees each.
seoDescription: Cairn AI agents attacked more than 1,100 sites from open dashboards, NorForge found. Costs near 50 dollars per break in and the boring holes they used.

image.alt: A Neuron illustration of a smiling cat with a magnifying glass beside a laptop labeled Agent Control, with an unlocked padlock and the words AI Hackers Left Their Dashboards Wide Open
image.subject: Cairn AI hackers open dashboard illustration
image.credit: Image: Illustration via The Neuron. Story source: The Neuron, October 20, 2026

sections.heading: A team of AI workers sharing one whiteboard
paragraphs: Security startup NorForge found more than 20 control panels for an AI hacking tool called Cairn sitting open on the public internet, with no password needed to read them. The Neuron reports that the panels appear to belong to criminals, and they offer a rare look inside how crooks are now using AI agents to break into real businesses.

Cairn works like a small crew sharing a whiteboard. A human gives the agents a target and a goal, such as breaking into one online store, and that job becomes a project. The agents post what they learn and what they plan to try next on the shared board, and because the board remembers everything, a single project can keep running for hours or even days.

sections.heading: The scale is what should worry site owners
paragraphs: One cluster of 14 panels, driven by instructions written in Chinese, held more than 1,100 attack projects aimed mostly at online stores in the United States, Japan, and Australia. The Rundown puts the same operation at more than 1,200 sites targeted, with one operator appearing to compromise more than 100 companies, including names reported by Reuters and The Verge such as Cummins, Deere, and SharkNinja.

NorForge estimates about 10 percent of projects hit their goal, and the successful ones in that cluster took just under 23 hours on average from start to finish. A typical attempt cost roughly 5 dollars in model fees once failures are counted, which works out to roughly 50 dollars in model fees per successful break in.

sections.heading: They verified at least one break in was real
paragraphs: Skepticism is fair here, because dashboards can exaggerate. NorForge checked one claimed break in at a large hardware parts vendor and found the back door, a hidden page that lets attackers upload files to a site server, still sitting live on the vendor site. That is not a simulation. That is a real hole left open in a real store.

The exposed panels also leaked the attackers own secrets. Scanning them turned up hundreds of exposed passwords and access keys, and 11 percent were still valid. One group even posted the login for its own staging server. The people threatening company security forgot to lock their own command center.

sections.heading: The holes were boring, and that is the point
paragraphs: The agents were not inventing science fiction exploits. Their work list was the boring stuff that site owners have been warned about for years:
bullets: Login flaws and pages that skip the login check entirely
File upload pages that let strangers place code on a server
Old known holes that stay unpatched while owners stay busy
Worker names in the panels suggest common coding agents powered by the cheap DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model, though NorForge calls that its reading and not a confirmed fact

sections.heading: What a Florida business should do this week
paragraphs: If you run a website, a store, or a client portal, treat this as a maintenance alarm. Update the site and its plugins, close upload and login holes, change any password that was ever shared loosely, and ask anyone who tests your security how they protect their own AI dashboards. NorForge says even apparently legitimate testing setups were left exposed, which can leak a client secrets.

Keep the numbers in proportion. NorForge sells tools for containing AI agents, its 10 percent figure is its own estimate, and success varies by group. But the direction is clear: old holes now get found faster, because software can work through more than a thousand projects without getting tired. Boring maintenance just became a real competitive edge.

sources.title: The Neuron: AI hackers left the door open (October 20, 2026)
The Rundown AI: One hacker AI agents break into 100 plus companies (October 20, 2026)

title: Three Trays of Baklava Became a 70,000 Dollar Month
excerpt: Jacob Komarow tripled his money selling three trays of baklava at a Phish concert on a bet. The Hustle Blower follows Good Baklava to nearly 70,000 dollars in December 2025 sales, under 10,000 dollars the next month, and no regular salary for the founder.
seoDescription: Good Baklava went from a concert bet to nearly 70,000 dollars in December sales, then under 10,000 in January. The sourcing, free samples, and revenue lesson.

image.alt: A metal tray of glossy pistachio topped baklava pieces from Good Baklava, cut in neat rows and sprinkled with ground green pistachio
image.subject: Good Baklava pistachio tray
image.credit: Image: Good Baklava pistachio baklava tray photo via Good Baklava. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 18, 2026

sections.heading: It all started with a concert, a bet, and three trays
paragraphs: In September 2021, Jacob Komarow was on his way to a Phish concert in California when he stopped at a Middle Eastern grocery store and spotted baklava, the layered pastry packed with nuts and soaked in sweet syrup. He bought three trays. His friend did not think he could sell them at the concert.

Jacob sold every piece and, by his account, walked away with three times what he had spent. Most people would take the win and move on. Instead, for nearly three years he sold baklava at concerts, parks, and festivals, anywhere he could find people looking for a good time and a good snack. No storefront, no venture capital, no new technology. Just a product people already loved, brought to a place where nobody else was selling it.

sections.heading: Plot twist: the Baklava Guy does not make baklava
paragraphs: You would expect a man nicknamed the Baklava Guy to spend his mornings covered in flour. He does not. In 2022, Jacob connected with a supplier through a Turkish food vendor in Paterson, New Jersey. Today, Good Baklava sources its pastries from a bakery in Gaziantep, Turkey, a city famous for its baklava, and a commercial baker in New Jersey handles the baking.

Jacob focuses on the other side of the equation: getting people to buy it. He did not invent the product, open a bakery, or become a pastry chef. He built a business around finding a quality product, sourcing it well, and making the buying experience memorable. Imported food still brings logistics, storage, safety requirements, and inventory costs, so this is no effortless fantasy. It is a distribution and attention business with a dessert at the center.

sections.heading: His next marketing strategy was giving it away
paragraphs: In 2026, Jacob started handing out free baklava outside Madison Square Garden, including to basketball fans celebrating in the streets. It was random, it was funny, and it was exactly the kind of moment people pull out their phones to film.

Videos circulated online, media attention followed, brands started exploring partnerships, and a major newspaper profiled him. The Hustle Blower makes the distinction clearly: Jacob was not just giving away dessert, he was giving people a story to tell. Free samples can destroy margins when they generate nothing, but Jacob had spent years learning how to work a crowd, and the internet gave that experience a much bigger audience.

sections.heading: The 70,000 dollar month and the January hangover
paragraphs: According to CNBC Make It reporting based on reviewed business records, Good Baklava averaged a little over 20,000 dollars in monthly sales during a recent nine month period. Then December 2025 arrived, with holiday gift buying and a temporary booth at the Union Square Holiday Market:
bullets: December 2025 reached nearly 70,000 dollars in sales, the best month in the story
January 2026 fell to less than 10,000 dollars, a drop of more than 85 percent
At reporting time, three pieces sold for around 10 dollars in person and an online 12 pack listed for about 30 dollars
Despite the growth, Jacob said he still was not paying himself a regular salary, with a goal of about 4,000 dollars a month by the end of 2026

sections.heading: Revenue is not profit, and seasons are real
paragraphs: December is gift season and holiday markets bring enormous foot traffic. A random Tuesday in January brings neither. Rent, insurance, and inventory do not disappear when sales collapse, which is why a best month can make a founder feel rich while the worst month shows what the business actually needs to survive.

For Florida food and event sellers, the playbook is useful. Take a proven product to crowds already gathered, from concerts to holiday markets. Let free samples buy attention when the moment is filmable. Then build the boring parts, sourcing, permits, and a salary for yourself, before January arrives.

title: A Free Run Club Made 640,000 Dollars From What Happened After the Run
excerpt: Owen Akhibi Herrera started Peak and Pace with 12 runners in New York and kept the Saturday runs free. The Hustle Blower reports the money came from ticketed parties and trips after the run, passing 640,000 dollars in revenue in 2025.
seoDescription: Peak and Pace free run club passed 640,000 dollars in 2025 revenue from 20 dollar parties and trips, not memberships. The ferry breakdown and the events lesson.

image.alt: Members of the Peak and Pace run club posing together outdoors in running gear with the New York skyline and picnic tables behind them
image.subject: Peak and Pace run club members
image.credit: Image: Peak and Pace run club photo via Peak and Pace. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 19, 2026

sections.heading: It began with 12 people looking for friends
paragraphs: In July 2024, Owen Akhibi Herrera was a London transplant living in New York and working in algorithmic trading sales at an investment bank. His problem was one money could not easily solve: making genuine friends as an adult is surprisingly difficult. So he organized a Saturday morning run, and 12 people showed up.

Owen kept going. He posted about the group on social media every day, encouraged people to bring friends, and made the experience welcoming enough that newcomers did not feel like they had wandered into Olympic training camp. By the fifth run, around 150 people were showing up. A dozen strangers had become a crowd big enough to fill a small nightclub, except they were wearing running shoes at 9 in the morning.

sections.heading: The money was never in the run
paragraphs: The clever part is what Owen did not do. He did not announce that Saturday runs would now cost money. He did not launch a premium membership or put the community behind a paywall. The activity that attracted everyone stayed completely free.

Instead, he tested what happened after the run. He organized a party at a Manhattan bar and charged roughly 20 dollars a ticket, and people bought tickets. Want to run? Come free. Want to party with the people you have been running with? Grab a ticket. Want a bigger adventure? There is a hiking trip or a ski trip for that. The Hustle Blower puts it plainly: he did not monetize the run, he monetized the relationships the run created.

sections.heading: The numbers, with the honest asterisk
paragraphs: By 2025, Peak and Pace had recorded more than 30,000 event attendances across its gatherings, counting repeat visitors, and financial documents reviewed by CNBC showed the business bringing in more than 640,000 dollars in revenue that year. Tickets to larger parties typically cost 15 to 25 dollars, while the weekly runs remained free.
Revenue is not profit, and this story keeps that front and center:
bullets: Owen says Peak and Pace operates at around a 15 percent profit margin, roughly 96,000 dollars on that revenue
He reinvests the profits into the company rather than paying himself a second salary
A 150 person party at 20 dollars a ticket grosses 3,000 dollars before venue, DJ, security, staff, insurance, and fees
Some individual events actually lose money

sections.heading: Then the ferry broke down
paragraphs: On September 5, 2025, Owen was preparing one of his biggest events yet: a 5K race and festival on Governors Island, just off Manhattan. Two thousand people had bought tickets, and his team had organized 18 trucks loaded with equipment that all needed to cross the water.

Then the ferry broke down. After hours of frantic phone calls, Owen arranged replacement transportation, and the final shipment, roughly 30 portable toilets, arrived just as guests were reaching the island. People see the packed events and smiling faces online. They do not see the founder wondering whether a festival is about to collapse because the bathrooms are stuck on the wrong side of the river.

sections.heading: What Florida event builders should steal
paragraphs: The model translates directly. Free and easy gets people in the door and gives them a reason to return every week. Paid and special is what they buy once they belong. A free photo walk, a free creator meetup, or a free community workout can do in Tampa or Orlando what a free run did in New York, if the paid experience waiting after it is genuinely worth having.

Start with getting 12 strangers into the same place, give them a reason to come back, and pay attention to what they want next. The most valuable thing you build might not be the thing you charge for. Just make sure you have a backup ferry.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: The 640K Business Behind Free Runs (October 19, 2026)

title: Anthropic Wants to Give the Public Five Percent of Itself
excerpt: Anthropic introduced a Public Benefit Fund that would hold 5 percent of the company equity, worth about 48 billion dollars at its May valuation, and could send direct distributions to groups like workers hit by AI. The Rundown explains the plan.
seoDescription: Anthropic Public Benefit Fund would hold 5 percent of equity, about 48 billion dollars, for nonprofits and workers hit by AI. The Rundown on how it grows.

image.alt: Anthropic artwork for its Investing in the public benefit announcement dated October 18, 2026, showing framed panels of blue sky and a flower meadow facing each other
image.subject: Anthropic public benefit artwork
image.credit: Image: Artwork via Anthropic. Story source: The Rundown AI, October 19, 2026

sections.heading: Real stock behind a familiar promise
paragraphs: Frontier AI labs keep saying the money AI makes should be shared with the public, but so far that has mostly lived in research papers and warnings. The Rundown reports that Anthropic just put real stock behind the idea.

Anthropic introduced a Public Benefit Fund that would get 5 percent of the company equity if shareholders sign off. At its May valuation, that stake is worth about 48 billion dollars. The fund is structured as a company owned LLC, and Anthropic says it could back nonprofits or make direct distributions to specific populations, with no stock going to lobbying or politics.

sections.heading: How the fund grows as Anthropic grows
paragraphs: The design ties public benefit to company value instead of fixing a one time gift. Each 50 percent jump in Anthropic value past an unannounced baseline could add 2 percent more equity at the board discretion. The Rundown frames that as Anthropic answer to the growing executive pay scales in tech: as insiders get richer, the public share is supposed to climb too.

One named target is close to home for a lot of readers. Anthropic identified AI toll on workers as one focus, building on 200 million dollars it committed in June to study job disruption and test policy responses. Counting the new fund, the cofounders pledge of 80 percent of their own wealth giving, and stock it matches when staff donate, Anthropic now counts about 20 percent of its shares as set aside for public good.

sections.heading: The same company is changing its own workforce
paragraphs: The Rundown paired the fund news with a second Anthropic story that makes the first one feel less abstract. Anthropic published a study of its own workforce and found that employees agents logged six times the hours of the people running them by August, while junior roles shrank as a share of technical hiring:
bullets: Juniors went from 27 percent of Anthropic technical hires to just 9 percent
About a third of its machine learning managers said AI had them hiring less
Engineers push five times the code changes they did six months earlier, with agent code rolled back no more often than human code was
Claude agents sit idle about 80 percent of the time in work sessions while waiting on a person to respond

sections.heading: Why the two stories belong together
paragraphs: Read together, the picture is honest about the trade. Inside one of the top AI labs, agents are producing more than staff can read, entry level doors are narrowing, and experienced staff are moving departments far more often than a year ago. Anthropic is building AI risk alerts per role to move people toward less exposed jobs inside the company.

That internal reality is exactly what a public benefit fund claims to answer at society scale. If AI raises productivity by shrinking the number of people needed to do the work, who shares in the value that productivity creates? A fund that can send money directly to workers hit by AI is one concrete answer, even if it is still only a design today.

sections.heading: What to watch before calling it real
paragraphs: The Rundown lands on the right caution. Universal basic income and other public benefit structures have been floated throughout the AI age, and this fund plus the OpenAI foundation are the clearest signs yet of labs putting real equity behind the talk. But until money actually reaches anyone, it will be hard for the public to separate these moves from a convenient public relations play.

Public trust in AI is sliding, and cash in people hands might do more than another essay ever could. For creators, the lesson is simpler: build skills that sit on the judgment side of the work, and watch whether this fund ever writes its first real check.
