title: Meta New Terms Could Let It Scrape Your Business Website
excerpt: Meta business terms taking effect October 30 authorize scraping websites associated with businesses that use its products, The Neuron reports. If you share an article on Instagram, experts say Meta could collect the full article from your own site.
seoDescription: Meta business terms effective October 30 could authorize scraping business websites for AI training, experts told Nieman Lab. What creators and publishers should know.

image.alt: A Neuron illustration of a surprised cat at a laptop while a robotic arm with the Meta logo lifts a page from a stack labeled Terms, under the words Meta new terms could let it scrape your website
image.subject: Meta website scraping terms illustration
image.credit: Image: Illustration via The Neuron. Story source: The Neuron, October 18, 2026

sections.heading: You use Instagram to send people to your work
paragraphs: Most Florida creators and event brands use Instagram the same way. You post the clip, you share the flyer, and you point people back to your own website, where your articles, prices, and booking pages live under your control. The Neuron reports that the fine print behind that routine is about to change.

Meta business terms take effect October 30 and authorize scraping websites associated with businesses using its products. Scraping here means automatically collecting content from those sites, and Meta says the purpose includes developing and training Meta products.

sections.heading: The reach could go beyond what you post
paragraphs: This is the part that should make publishers sit up. Legal experts told Nieman Lab, as reported by The Neuron, that the terms could include training Meta AI on publishers articles. Sharing an article on Instagram could authorize Meta to collect the full article from your site, under the experts reading of the terms.

In other words, the content at risk is not only the photo or caption you uploaded. It can be the page you linked to, on a website you own, written for your audience. And according to Nieman Lab, you cannot reject these terms separately and keep using Meta business products. Accepting the platform and accepting the scraping arrive as one package.

sections.heading: Meta says it is simpler than it sounds
paragraphs: Meta says the update is about ads and recommendations, simplifying existing rules for collecting product information, not claiming a new right to scrape news. That explanation may be sincere, and it is also exactly why the wording matters. A company can describe a narrow intention today while holding broad permission tomorrow.

The Neuron adds useful context: even if Meta has permission to collect content, using that content to train AI is a separate legal question about whether it has the right to learn from the work. Five major publishers sued Meta in May, alleging it pirated millions of works to train its Llama AI models. That case is separate, but it shows why a new set of terms does not end the argument over whose work AI can learn from.

sections.heading: What this means for your own site
paragraphs: None of this means you should delete Instagram tomorrow. For most event and creative businesses in Florida, Instagram is still where the audience lives, and leaving has a real cost. It does mean your website strategy should be clear eyed:
bullets: Know that linking your site from business accounts may carry broader permission than most owners realize
Keep your most valuable original work easy to find on your own domain, where your name and offers sit beside it
Read the October 30 terms for your own accounts instead of relying on summaries, including this one

sections.heading: The bigger question underneath
paragraphs: AI companies are hungry for training data, and platforms control the doors most small businesses walk through to reach customers. When the door owner also wants to learn from everything you carry through it, the bargain deserves a hard look.

The practical takeaway is ownership. Build the audience where you can, but build the asset where you control it: your site, your list, and your direct relationships. Platforms can change their terms on a date they choose. The work you publish under your own name is still yours, and posts like this one will keep tracking what that protection is actually worth.

sources.title: The Neuron: Use Meta for business? Check these terms (October 18, 2026)

title: A Free DeepSeek Model Edged Opus 5 at Coding
excerpt: DeepSeek released a downloadable model update that scored 77.0 on a coding agent test, ahead of Claude Opus 5 at 74.0, and opened web search tools priced about 85 percent below rivals. The Neuron breaks down what is real and what is marketing.
seoDescription: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scored 77.0 on DeepSWE, edging Opus 5, with free weights and search at 0.75 dollars per 1,000 calls. The Neuron story and the caveats.

image.alt: A Neuron illustration of a smiling cat at a laptop beside code and web search graphics, with a price tag reading 0.75 dollars and the words DeepSeek new model and 85 percent cheaper search
image.subject: DeepSeek cheaper search illustration
image.credit: Image: Illustration via The Neuron. Story source: The Neuron, October 19, 2026

sections.heading: A new brain and a pair of eyes, priced like a clearance sale
paragraphs: On Saturday, DeepSeek released two things at once, according to The Neuron. The first is a model update called V4.1 Flash 1017. The second is public access to its own web Search and Fetch tools for AI agents. One gives an agent a better brain. The other gives it a way to look things up.

The model update matters because of how it is distributed. The weights are free to download under an MIT license, so anyone can run the model or build a paid service on top of it. That is a very different offer from a model you can only rent from one company, one month at a time.

sections.heading: The coding score everyone will quote
paragraphs: On DeepSWE v1.1, a coding agent test, DeepSeek reports a score of 77.0, versus 74.0 for Claude Opus 5 and 73.0 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Those are the numbers that will travel, and The Neuron is careful about how far they should travel.
The fine print deserves equal billing:
bullets: DeepSeek ran those tests itself, so independent confirmation is still pending
Opus 5 still wins on Humanity Last Exam, 56.3 to 42.6, and on Terminal Bench 4.0, 51.8 to 42.3
The honest reading is a great value coder, not a new smartest model overall

sections.heading: The price gap is the real story
paragraphs: DeepSeek charges 0.15 dollars per million input tokens and 0.60 dollars per million output tokens off peak. In August, Artificial Analysis found the earlier Flash model cost about 3 cents to run its whole test suite, versus 1.86 dollars for GPT 5.6 Sol and 3.15 dollars for Claude Fable 5. Three cents for work that cost dollars elsewhere changes what small teams can afford to automate.

The new Search and Fetch tools push the same point. Search returns ranked results for a query, and Fetch opens a page and returns its text in a clean format agents can read. Each costs 0.75 dollars per 1,000 successful requests, and failed or empty calls are free. One pricing roundup cited by The Neuron lists rivals at 5 dollars per 1,000 and up, which is where the roughly 85 percent gap in the headline comes from.

sections.heading: Why open weights squeeze everyone else
paragraphs: The Neuron argues that open weights cap prices across the market, because any cloud provider can host the model, and OpenRouter already lists about a dozen hosts for it. The top closed models still look safe on the hardest reasoning work, so the squeeze lands first on bulk work like routine coding and long agent loops, exactly the work that burns the most tokens.

There is also a geopolitics layer creators should at least know exists. United States agencies have accused DeepSeek of training on other models outputs at industrial scale, Beijing has pushed back, and China has proposed export controls on very large AI models. DeepSeek shipped this release on the safe side of that proposed line: open weights for a mid size model, and a paid API for the rest.

sections.heading: What a Florida creator should do with this
paragraphs: Treat this as a budget tool, not a belief system. Public web research, first pass coding help, and bulk sorting are reasonable jobs for a cheap open model. Keep confidential client material out of it, since Search and Fetch run on DeepSeek servers and several governments restrict DeepSeek on official devices over data security.

Watch two things The Neuron flags: November 1, when the free window for calls through tools like Claude Code and Codex ends and real bills begin, and whether anyone independent can reproduce that 77.0 coding score. If both land well, the price of getting AI help just dropped again, and small studios that move early will feel it first.

sources.title: The Neuron: DeepSeek free model edged Opus 5 at coding (October 19, 2026)

title: Basketball Stars Are Building Real Businesses With Podcasts and Streams
excerpt: Morning Brew rounds up the NBA and WNBA players running podcasts and Twitch streams, from the StudBudz to All the Smoke, and reports top shows can earn seven figures. For role players, the mic can outpay the game.
seoDescription: NBA and WNBA stars are building podcast and streaming businesses, from StudBudz to Draymond Green. Morning Brew on the seven figure shows and the creator lesson.

image.alt: Minnesota Lynx players Natisha Hiedeman in a pink tracksuit and Courtney Williams in a black jersey and sunglasses, the StudBudz streamers, posing together against a red dotted wall
image.subject: StudBudz Natisha Hiedeman and Courtney Williams
image.credit: Image: The StudBudz, Natisha Hiedeman and Courtney Williams, photo by Steph Chambers via Getty Images. Story source: Morning Brew, October 18, 2026

sections.heading: The second career starts while the first one is still playing
paragraphs: Current or retired, superstar or role player, a striking number of NBA and WNBA players now run popular podcasts or Twitch streams, sometimes with relatives, historians, and other experts at the table. Morning Brew frames these shows as side hustles, but the scale in its roundup suggests something bigger: players are building media businesses they own, on schedules they control.

The audience logic is simple. Fans already trust these voices on the game, and a stream or podcast lets a player talk for hours in a way a postgame interview never allows. Personality, access, and consistency turn playing fame into a direct audience relationship that does not retire when a playing career does.

sections.heading: The shows Morning Brew says are worth your time
paragraphs: The roundup spans both leagues and several formats, from teammate streams to veteran interview shows:
bullets: The StudBudz on Twitch, with Minnesota Lynx players Courtney Williams and Natisha Hiedeman
The Draymond Green Show, plus Club 520 with Jeff Teague, DJ Wells, and Bishop Henn
All the Smoke with Matt Barnes and Stephen Jackson, and Birds Eye View with Sue Bird
Straight to Cam with Cameron Brink and Sydel Curry Lee, and the Roommates Show with Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart

sections.heading: When the podcast outearns the playing career
paragraphs: Morning Brew cites The Hollywood Reporter reporting that a podcast hosted by someone of Draymond Greens stature can earn seven figures. For a star earning 27.7 million dollars this season, that is welcome money. For a role player, it can be the main event.

Matt Barnes, who was more of a role player during his career, said he expects to make more from podcasting than he made from the NBA. Read that twice. The league gave him the credibility and the stories. The show he built himself is what converts them into long term income, on his own terms, long after the final contract ends.

sections.heading: What athletes in Florida should copy right now
paragraphs: You do not need a national audience to use this playbook. A high school standout, a college player, or a local pro can start with the same ingredients: one repeatable format, one honest point of view, and a posting rhythm that survives a busy season. A weekly show recorded with a teammate costs little, compounds fast, and gives sponsors something concrete to buy besides a jersey.

The deeper lesson is ownership. A team controls your minutes, your role, and eventually your roster spot. Nobody can cut you from your own channel. Players who treat content as a business while they play are not chasing attention. They are building the asset that will still be working for them when the game moves on, and that is a plan any creator can respect.

title: A Nobel Economist Helped WNBA Players Win a Historic Pay Raise
excerpt: Claudia Goldin does not watch basketball, but she knows a wage gap when she sees one. Morning Brew reports how her viewer math helped WNBA players secure a 400 percent pay bump, with average pay rising toward 583,000 dollars.
seoDescription: Nobel economist Claudia Goldin advised the WNBA players union and helped win a 400 percent pay raise. The viewer math, the new average salary, and what comes next.

image.alt: Economist Claudia Goldin smiling as she holds her Nobel Prize medal in an open case on a stage decorated with flowers
image.subject: Claudia Goldin with her Nobel Prize
image.credit: Image: Claudia Goldin receiving her Nobel Prize in 2023, photo by Christine Olsson via Getty Images. Story source: Morning Brew, October 18, 2026

sections.heading: The economist who does not watch basketball
paragraphs: Nobel Prize winning economist Claudia Goldin says she does not watch basketball. Morning Brew reports that she still knew a wage gap when she saw one, and that she used her expertise in gender pay disparities to advise the WNBA players union during salary negotiations last year.

The result was an unprecedented raise the newsletter puts at 400 percent. Goldin helped crunch the numbers behind the players claim that their pay did not reflect the leagues rising popularity, a surge turbocharged by stars like Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese and visible in the leagues best regular season viewership since 2000.

sections.heading: The viewer math that made the case
paragraphs: Goldin dug into television ratings to argue that the WNBA average yearly paycheck of 127,000 dollars in 2024, compared with an NBA average of 10 million dollars, was an embarrassing wage gap. Her core calculation reframed the comparison around audience per player instead of raw league size:
bullets: The WNBA attracted about 30 percent as many monetizable broadcast viewers per player as the NBA, accounting for the number and length of games
Per player game attendance showed a similar pattern, by her analysis
On that basis she argued equitable WNBA salaries would average a third to a quarter of NBA paychecks
She also rejected the idea that the gap simply reflects profitability, noting the leagues costly expansion shows investors see it as lucrative

sections.heading: What the new deal actually pays
paragraphs: Soon after, the league and the union signed a contract bumping the players estimated average annual salary to 583,000 dollars, expected to rise to more than one million dollars by 2032. Other economists seconded Goldins findings, and Morning Brew notes a structural point worth remembering: the NBA spends about 50 percent of its revenue on player salaries, while WNBA paychecks have represented a much smaller fraction of league revenue.

The momentum behind the deal is still building. The WNBA is among the fastest growing sports leagues in the United States, viewership grew 17 percent last season, and the league plans to reach 18 teams by 2030, six more than it had in 2024. Skeptics question whether the growth rate can hold, and that question will decide how the next negotiation feels.

sections.heading: Why this matters beyond basketball
paragraphs: Every creative industry has a version of this negotiation. Photographers, videographers, editors, and performers are often told the exposure is the payment, or that the budget simply is what it is. Goldins contribution was not a slogan. It was a fair comparison, built from audience numbers anyone could check, that made the old pay scale impossible to defend with a straight face.

The practical lesson is to bring receipts in the right unit. Count the audience your work actually draws, the revenue it helps create, and the share that flows to the people creating it, then put those three numbers side by side before you talk price. That is how a pay conversation stops being a favor request and becomes an accounting question, and it works in a league office or at a Florida event venue.

sources.title: Morning Brew: Basketball Brew, The Nobel winner behind the WNBA historic pay raise (October 18, 2026)

title: EATABLE Turned Popcorn Into a Million Dollar Gift Business
excerpt: Charlene and Vince Li gave a cheap snack a completely different job: a giftable, celebratory treat in dark dramatic packaging. The Hustle Blower follows EATABLE from 56,000 dollars in year one to more than 1,600 stores.
seoDescription: EATABLE popcorn crossed a million dollars in annual revenue and 1,600 stores by repositioning a cheap snack as a premium gift. The Instagram retail breakthrough inside.

image.alt: Five colorful bags of EATABLE gourmet popcorn standing in an open gift box printed with the words Flavour Trip Inside, surrounded by travel props
image.subject: EATABLE gourmet popcorn gift box
image.credit: Image: EATABLE gourmet popcorn gift box photo via EATABLE. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 18, 2026

sections.heading: The idea began on movie night
paragraphs: In 2018, Charlene and Vince Li were living in Boston with a young child. Charlene came from finance and accounting, Vince from technology sales and real estate, and neither had built a packaged food company. Looking for something special to serve while entertaining or watching a movie, they found grocery shelves full of snacks and nothing quite right.

Vince experimented with a stovetop caramel popcorn recipe and developed a premium, grown up flavor concept. The detail that mattered was not the recipe alone. It was the occasion. They were not competing with the cheapest movie popcorn. They were building a giftable, celebratory snack that felt like a small luxury, and that one decision changed everything from the packaging to the customer.

sections.heading: Dad was the first customer. A stranger was the real test.
paragraphs: The couple learned the food business basics through a Boston incubator, tested an early flavor with food professionals, then moved back to Toronto, worked with pastry specialists, and refined the product. They chose dark, dramatic packaging that looked nothing like a typical supermarket bag, developed three initial recipes, and opened an online store in 2019.

Charlene has said her first customer was her father, which is lovely and also not product market fit. The milestone that counted came later, when an order arrived from a name she did not recognize. A stranger had seen the product, understood the proposition, and paid for it. That first unknown buyer proves more than a hundred supportive relatives ever will.

sections.heading: Instagram put them on retail shelves
paragraphs: Working on the business part time, the couple reported 56,000 dollars in revenue in year one. About six months in, major retailers found them through Instagram and started carrying the popcorn, because a product that looks distinctive enough to stop a scroll can also make sense on a physical shelf. The retailer was not just buying popcorn. It was buying something different to put in front of shoppers.
The climb that followed, as reported by The Hustle Blower:
bullets: Year two reportedly reached 467,000 dollars in revenue, and year three reached 893,000 dollars
The company eventually crossed one million dollars in annual revenue
In a March 2025 interview the founders described sales through more than 1,600 retail locations in Canada and the United States
Those are company sales, not personal profit, and the growth carried real manufacturing risk

sections.heading: The batch that almost broke a retail order
paragraphs: Outside manufacturers could not easily reproduce the couples specialized process, so they developed their own production facility of 3,000 square feet, supported by a government backed bank loan. Later, a batch made by an outside manufacturer failed their standards right before a major retail shipment. The texture was wrong and the coating was inconsistent, so they would not send it.

Instead, they worked overtime in their own facility and told the retail partner about the problem. That is not the moment founders put in a launch video. It is the moment that decides whether a retailer orders again. Premium positioning survives only when the product inside matches the promise outside.

sections.heading: Sell the occasion, not the commodity
paragraphs: A cheap commodity competes on price. A premium gift competes on story, presentation, novelty, and occasion. EATABLE later developed custom products for major entertainment brands and events, but the lesson travels without a famous partner: a product gets easier to sell when buyers can immediately imagine the moment they will use it, give it, or serve it.

Florida creators and event brands can run the same play. Take a familiar item, name the exact occasion it belongs to, package it so the occasion is visible at a glance, and protect your margins when retail comes calling. The couple changed the question from how to make cheaper popcorn to when someone would be excited to give popcorn as a gift. A different question built a different business.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: How Popcorn Became Their 1M Business (October 18, 2026)

title: A Teenager Sold 808,000 Dollars of a Plastic Can Holder
excerpt: Michael Satterlee turned a can holder that pops an empty can out when a fresh one goes in into 808,000 dollars of gross revenue in 2025. The Hustle Blower tells the viral video story, and the printer bottleneck hiding behind it.
seoDescription: Cruise Cup did 808,000 dollars in 2025 gross revenue from a 3D printed can holder. The 50 million view demo, the 315,000 dollar month, and the operations lesson.

image.alt: A black Cruise Cup tactical reload can holder with a silver drink can seated in the top, photographed on a white background
image.subject: Cruise Cup tactical reload can holder
image.credit: Image: Cruise Cup tactical reload can holder product photo via Cruise Cup. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 17, 2026

sections.heading: He started with printers he already owned
paragraphs: Michael Satterlee built Cruise Cup selling something that sounds like a joke: a plastic holder for a drink can. By the numbers The Hustle Blower reports, the joke stopped being funny fast. The business generated 808,000 dollars in gross revenue in 2025, including one month at 315,000 dollars in sales.

Michael was not starting from zero. In high school in Clifton Park, New York, his earlier company Solefully designed and printed accessories for clogs, teaching him product design, 3D printing, online sales, social media, and shipping. It also left him with printers that were not busy all the time, so instead of buying equipment for a new idea, he asked what else the machines he already owned could make.

sections.heading: The improvement you can understand with the sound off
paragraphs: He chose insulated drink sleeves, a familiar category where he did not have to convince anyone the product should exist. He only had to give people a reason to buy a different one. His hard shell holder accepts a can from either end, and he refined it so that pressing it onto a fresh can pops the empty one out.

That tiny mechanism became a built in performance. According to Michaels January 2026 interview with Entrepreneur, a demonstration video drew roughly 50 million views. Watch someone finish a drink, press the holder onto a fresh can, and watch the empty one pop out. The whole selling point lands in seconds, with the sound turned off. A boring object had become something worth filming, which is exactly the kind of product short video rewards.

sections.heading: The month by month reality check
paragraphs: Cruise Cup launched in August 2025 and, by Michaels account, made about 100,000 dollars in its first month. Then the story gets more honest than most viral product tales:
bullets: September 2025 fell to about 55,000 dollars as organic reach weakened during paid advertising experiments
October 2025 returned to around 100,000 dollars, and November 2025 hit 315,000 dollars in sales
Gross revenue reached 808,000 dollars in 2025 and about 601,000 dollars through September 2026
Michael says he pays himself only 500 to 1,500 dollars a month and puts the rest back into equipment, marketing, and product development

sections.heading: The bottleneck was hiding inside the printer
paragraphs: Michael told Entrepreneur that one of his preferred desktop printers cost under 300 dollars, which makes the business sound easy to copy until you check the clock. One machine could make three signature holders in about 15 hours, roughly five printer hours per unit, or about five units a day running around the clock before breakdowns and handling.

Now picture a video sending hundreds of orders in a weekend, from customers who have already paid. By December he was so busy fulfilling holiday orders that he stopped running ads, and by October 2026 reporting described an operation using roughly 160 3D printers, plus people removing supports, packing, labeling, and shipping. The video created demand. Operations decided whether the business could keep it.

sections.heading: Copy the process, not the product
paragraphs: The Hustle Blower draws out five working rules: start with equipment and skills you already have, choose a category people already understand, add an improvement that can be demonstrated instantly, prototype and revise quickly, and treat comments as product research for the next version.

For creators, the translation is direct. Build the thing, the offer, or the scene so its value is obvious in the first three seconds of a clip, then make sure you can actually deliver what the clip sells. A sold out product with a five hour production time per unit can still be a hard business. The metric that matters is not views. It is profitable orders you can fulfill, week after week.

title: AI Meeting Notes Now Work in 32 Languages at Once
excerpt: The Neuron looks at the invisible tax language puts on global work, and at tools like Granola, whose meeting notes now follow conversations across 32 languages, accents, and mid sentence language switches.
seoDescription: Granola meeting notes now support 32 languages. The Neuron explains the participation, understanding, and memory problems multilingual AI can finally solve.

image.alt: A Neuron illustration of a cat at a laptop taking meeting notes while speech bubbles say hello in Spanish, English, Chinese, and Japanese above a video call
image.subject: The 32 language workplace illustration
image.credit: Image: Illustration via The Neuron. Story source: The Neuron, October 17, 2026

sections.heading: The meeting everyone understood only 80 percent of
paragraphs: Most companies already call themselves global. Their people sit in different countries, their customers speak different languages, and a single project can bounce between cities before lunch. Then everyone joins the meeting and quietly agrees to squeeze the whole company through one shared language, usually English.

The Neuron calls the cost of that squeeze an invisible tax. A person speaking a first language can jump in quickly, soften a disagreement, and improvise when the conversation turns. A person working in a second or third language is doing an extra job at the same time, translating the thought before contributing it. Technically fluent can quietly become understood most of it and nodded through the rest.

sections.heading: The problem was never just translation
paragraphs: The Neuron points to research on multinational teams that separates two kinds of friction. The obvious kind is vocabulary and grammar, where a missed word makes a point too hard to explain. The sneakier kind is tone, emphasis, and politeness habits carried from one language into another, which can change how the exact same sentence lands.

Add accents, local slang, product names, customer names, and internal acronyms, plus code switching, where someone moves between languages inside one sentence. A 2026 systematic review of code switching speech recognition found the field growing, but datasets, language coverage, and evaluation still uneven. Clean demo sentences are easy. Real work talk is not.

sections.heading: What Granola is doing with 32 languages
paragraphs: The sponsor example inside the deep dive is Granola, an AI notepad built for people who live in meetings. Its multi language mode is turned on once, and it then follows a conversation as it moves between languages, transcribing from your computer while you jot down what matters.

Afterward it turns the conversation plus your own notes into summaries, action items, and next steps. Under the hood that takes three jobs working in sequence: turning speech into text, detecting which language is being spoken as it changes, and then using a language model to turn the transcript and notes into a structured record of decisions, objections, owners, and dates.

sections.heading: Why the summary matters more than the transcript
paragraphs: A transcript is evidence. A summary is a shared object. The Neuron argues that the biggest loss in multilingual work often happens after the call, when a decision made in one language becomes a two sentence note in another, and three weeks later nobody remembers why option B won.
There is early evidence that lowering this friction changes behavior:
bullets: An NBER study found language barriers reduced interactions between foreign and domestic managers, and interactions rose when managers received English training
A smaller experiment found teams given machine translated logs of subgroup conversations before a main meeting showed better meeting quality
Structured notes let sales, product, and leadership each pull what they need from the original conversation instead of relying on one person retelling it

sections.heading: What Florida creators and small teams should take from this
paragraphs: You do not need a global company for this to matter. A Florida production team can brief a client in English, coordinate a vendor in Spanish, and deliver notes that both sides can search later. An event team can capture a planning call once and turn it into assignments instead of a chain of clarifying texts. The tool is not the point. The shared record is.

Keep the human limits in view. AI can capture a sentence perfectly and still miss what a polite refusal actually meant, and names and jargon will still break it. Let people speak in the language where they think best, let AI build the common record, and keep humans responsible for meaning when the stakes are high. That is the version of the 32 language workplace worth adopting.

sources.title: The Neuron: Deep Dive, The 32 language workplace is here (October 17, 2026)
Granola: The AI notepad for people in back to back meetings

excerpt: Tampa Bays favorite flea market opens its new season Saturday, October 17 at Campbell Park in St. Petersburg. Creative Loafing Tampa Bay reports 180 curated vendors, vintage collectors, artists, makers, designers, and local food for its 14th anniversary Grand Opening.
seoDescription: Indie Flea returns Saturday, October 17 at Campbell Park in St. Petersburg with 180 curated vendors for its 14th anniversary Grand Opening. What to expect.

sections.heading: Fourteen years of shopping small, back on Saturday
paragraphs: Indie Flea returns this Saturday, October 17, to Campbell Park in St. Petersburg for its 14th anniversary Grand Opening, according to Creative Loafing Tampa Bay. The market is bringing 180 curated vendors for the occasion, which is a serious footprint for a community market and a clear sign of how durable this format has become in Tampa Bay.

Creative Loafing describes Indie Flea as Tampa Bays favorite flea market, known for exceptional curation and vibrant community experiences. Fourteen years in, that reputation is the product. Shoppers trust that a Saturday at Indie Flea will be worth the trip before they know a single vendor name, and that kind of trust takes years of consistent selection to build.

sections.heading: What you will find among the 180 vendors
paragraphs: The lineup brings together the regions most sought after vintage collectors, artists, makers, designers, and independent brands. Expect an incredible selection of antiques and vintage treasures, with clothing, art, home goods, and one of a kind pieces that reward slow browsing.
The announcement also makes a point of the day beyond the shopping:
bullets: 180 curated vendors across vintage, art, design, and independent brands
Local food and beverage vendors picked for a family picnic on the grounds
A 14th anniversary Grand Opening that opens the new market season at Campbell Park in St. Petersburg

sections.heading: Why markets like this matter to Florida creators
paragraphs: A market at this scale is a working showcase for the local creative economy. Makers test products face to face with buyers, vintage sellers move pieces that would sit unseen online, and food vendors build the followings that carry them into their next location. For photographers and videographers, a crowd this colorful is also a portfolio day hiding in plain sight, with real people, real products, and real Florida light.

If you run a small brand in Tampa Bay, walking a market like Indie Flea is research you cannot get from a feed. Watch which booths hold a crowd, which displays stop people mid step, and which makers turn a browser into a buyer in under a minute. That is merchandising, storytelling, and pricing feedback happening live, all in one afternoon.

sections.heading: Plan the trip
paragraphs: Head to Campbell Park in St. Petersburg on Saturday, October 17, and give yourself time to browse slowly and stay for a picnic with your family, as the organizers suggest. Markets reward early arrivals for the best vintage finds and patient walkers for the small booths tucked between the big ones.

And if you are an organizer building something similar, study the formula: tight curation, a consistent home, food that keeps people on site, and a community that treats the date as a ritual. Fourteen years of Saturdays is not an accident. It is what happens when an event keeps its standard high enough that showing up stays an easy decision.

title: A Baby Shower Idea Became Artful Agenda at 275K a Month
excerpt: Katy Allen wanted a paper planner that could talk to a digital calendar. The Hustle Blower tells how she built a private group before the app, survived a developer disaster, and grew Artful Agenda to 275,000 dollars a month in gross revenue.
seoDescription: Artful Agenda grew from a baby shower conversation to 275K a month in gross revenue. The audience first playbook, the developer lesson, and the small pilot to copy.

image.alt: A tablet showing the Artful Agenda digital planner open to a colorful weekly calendar view with events, priorities, goals, and meal plans
image.subject: Artful Agenda digital planner weekly view
image.credit: Image: Artful Agenda planner on a tablet via Artful Agenda. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 16, 2026

sections.heading: The problem was a planner that could not sync
paragraphs: In Nashville in 2016, Katy Allen was raising young children, supporting a husband who traveled for work, and running a sales organization of more than 2,000 childrens book consultants. She loved beautiful paper planners, but her paper planner could not talk to her husbands digital calendar, and tools like Google Calendar synced appointments without giving her the planner experience she wanted.

At her daughters baby shower, a friend said she wished for a digital version of a beautiful paper agenda, and the light went on. One friend agreeing proves nothing on its own, but it told Katy the problem might live in other households too. She decided to find out properly before she built anything expensive.

sections.heading: She built the crowd before she built the app
paragraphs: Katy was not a software developer, so in 2017 she found people who understood software, sought business advice, and started learning. Her smartest move, though, involved no technology at all. She opened a private Facebook group for people who wanted a better digital planner, and she showed them mockups, features, designs, and pricing ideas.

Instead of guessing, she asked. The group became a research department that cost nothing, and when Artful Agenda finally launched, early testers from that group turned into paying subscribers. She was not collecting followers. She was recruiting future customers and product advisers at the same time, which is the kind of marketing any small team can copy.

sections.heading: A developer disaster, then a long climb
paragraphs: The hard chapter came with her first development company. By Katys account, the developers spent her budget while finishing only about half the app. She paid what was required to obtain the existing code, found a new team, and negotiated a fixed price arrangement with a local designer to get the product finished.

At launch the app brought in roughly 1,000 to 2,000 dollars a month, real money that still did not make the business profitable after development, support, and operating costs. Katy kept building and later invested in paid advertising, becoming profitable after about six months of ads. By June 2025 she reported far bigger numbers:
bullets: About 275,000 dollars in average monthly gross revenue
About 3.5 million dollars in annual gross revenue
All of it from a subscription product built around a problem she personally understood, with figures that are founder reported and not audited profit

sections.heading: Copy the order of operations, not the software bill
paragraphs: The Hustle Blower argues for reversing the usual sequence. Pick one specific group of people, talk to 20 of them about the task they hate, the copying between tools, and the mistakes that cost them time or money, and ask whether they have ever paid to make the problem go away. A complaint is not a market. A past payment is evidence of one.

Then sketch the fix with a mockup, a spreadsheet, or a template, and offer a small paid pilot you can deliver by hand. Twenty people paying 12 dollars is only 240 dollars, but it proves more than 500 likes ever will. Photographers juggling shoots, tutors juggling students, and event organizers juggling deadlines all live inside scheduling chaos every week. The audience first playbook works in Florida creative businesses exactly as well as it worked for a planner in Nashville.

title: Yardsale Made 220K in Three Months Selling Ski Poles Skiers Already Owned
excerpt: Cristina Ashbaugh found that 90 percent of skiers could not name their pole brand. The Hustle Blower tells how Yardsale turned that indifference into magnetic poles, 100K in first month sales, and a Shark Tank deal.
seoDescription: Yardsale ski poles did 220K in three months by fixing a forgotten accessory. The research question, the tape and magnets prototype, and the test to copy.

image.alt: A skier in leather gloves holding two red Yardsale ski poles clicked together by their magnetic handles, with the Yardsale name printed on the shafts
image.subject: Yardsale magnetic ski poles held together
image.credit: Image: Yardsale magnetic ski pole handles photo via Gear Patrol. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 17, 2026

sections.heading: Nobody could name the brand they already bought
paragraphs: Cristina Ashbaugh loved skiing but thought poles were inconvenient and boring, so in 2023 she started asking skiers two simple questions: what brand are your poles, and what feature do you like about them. In her informal research, 90 percent could not name the brand and 95 percent could not name a single thing they liked.

Ski shops told her the same story from the other side of the counter. Customers mostly chose poles by color, and salespeople had little to say about real differences. The category had customers, distribution, and money moving through it. What it did not have was affection, and that gap became the whole business case for Yardsale.

sections.heading: The first prototype was tape and magnets
paragraphs: Cristina teamed up with Kelly McGee, a former Apple product designer who had also started a medical device company. Their first experiment was delightfully plain: they taped magnets onto existing ski poles to see whether the poles would click together and become easier to carry through a parking lot in ski boots.

The click worked, and the improvement took about one second to understand. Turning that trick into a real product took serious work: hidden magnets in handles and baskets, modular parts, interchangeable colors, prototypes, factory meetings, tooling, and testing. The idea was easy to explain. Building it properly was not, and the founders are clear eyed about that difference.

sections.heading: Sales arrived before the television cameras did
paragraphs: In a January 2025 interview with Entrepreneur, Cristina reported 100,000 dollars in sales in the first month, 220,000 dollars in the first three months, and 300,000 dollars in the first year, which included a four month ski season. Those are founder reported sales, not audited profit, and the company carried inventory, manufacturing, fulfillment, and marketing costs.

Cristina described working her day job and then packing orders in Kellys basement at night, and after about ten days the founders decided the business deserved their full attention. Yardsale appeared on Shark Tank in November 2024 and reached an on air deal with guest investor Kendra Scott, but the early sales had already happened. The show amplified demand. It did not create the reason customers wanted the product.

sections.heading: Steal the forgotten accessory test, not the product
paragraphs: The Hustle Blower suggests hunting for the forgotten accessory in any hobby or trade: the small item people buy because they need it, never because they love it. List ten supporting products around an activity you know, then interview 20 real users about brand, annoyances, alternatives tried, and how they actually use the item.

Follow that with five retailers, instructors, or technicians, and ask what gets returned, what complaints repeat, and what customers improvise for themselves. If users and sellers name the same annoyance, a rough prototype built for about 150 dollars can test whether people understand it, use it, and ask the only question that counts: can I buy one. For creators, the same lens applies to the small frustrations inside a shoot day, an edit, or a booking process. Boring problems with a visible fix are often the best businesses in the room.

Gear Patrol: Yardsale magnetic ski poles (January 2025)

title: The Elizabeth Holmes Documentary That Could Make Oscars History
excerpt: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim followed Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she reported to prison. Morning Brew reports the A24 film opened to a 99 percent critics score and could become the first documentary ever nominated for best picture.
seoDescription: You Can See Everything, the Nathan Fielder film about Elizabeth Holmes, opened to a 99 percent critics score. Why it could make Oscars history for documentaries.

image.alt: Elizabeth Holmes in close up, smiling as she speaks with Nathan Fielder, whose back is to the camera, in a still from You Can See Everything
image.subject: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything
image.credit: Image: Still from You Can See Everything via A24 and The Playlist. Story source: Morning Brew, October 17, 2026

sections.heading: A secret film about the final weeks of freedom
paragraphs: You Can See Everything follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her incarceration, and it was made in near total secrecy. The three hour A24 film comes from comedian Nathan Fielder, working with co director Lance Oppenheim, and Morning Brew reports it hit theaters yesterday to a 99 percent critics rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

The Guardian called it more shocking, twistier, thornier, and more revealing than billed. That response matters because the project could easily have played as a stunt. Instead, critics are treating it as a serious portrait of a person who built a fraud on confidence, filmed by a performer whose whole career studies how people perform.

sections.heading: Not a rescue mission, a study of a character
paragraphs: Morning Brew stresses that this film is not Fielder trying to save a failed business, which is the engine of much of his earlier work. He spends time living alongside Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, in the days before her imprisonment, trying to understand her elusive character. He ends up as the last person she hugs before she is driven away to begin her 11 year sentence.
The details around the edges are revealing on their own:
bullets: Evans tries, without success, to negotiate a cut of the film proceeds for Holmes
Evans admits he does not run some posts on Holmes social account by her first while she is in prison
After Holmes reports to prison, Fielder brings in Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy playing Holmes in The Dropout, to reenact his odd conversations with her

sections.heading: Why the Oscars talk is not just hype
paragraphs: Hollywood watchers quoted by Morning Brew say the buzz and the critical response could make this the first documentary ever nominated for best picture in the nearly 100 year history of the award. Documentaries have won major honors for decades, but the top category has stayed closed to them. A nomination would redraw what the industry thinks a documentary can be.

The path here is worth studying for any filmmaker. The film was kept under wraps until a trailer arrived last month showing an unblinking Holmes assuring Fielder of her honesty. Secrecy, timing, and one unforgettable image did the marketing work that a long campaign usually buys.

sections.heading: What documentary makers in Florida can learn
paragraphs: Access is the whole game in documentary work, and access is earned with patience and trust, not with a bigger camera. Fielder got scenes nobody else could get because he stayed present for the small days, not only the dramatic ones. Event filmmakers and brand storytellers work the same muscle every time they follow a founder, an artist, or a team through a real process.

The second lesson is restraint in the reveal. This team held its footage, finished its film, and let one strong trailer open the conversation. If you are sitting on powerful footage right now, resist posting it in pieces. Build the finished piece, choose the single scene that proves its value, and let that scene carry the launch.

title: KFC Ends 40 Years With Pepsi and Switches to Coca Cola
excerpt: After 40 years serving Pepsi products in its US restaurants, KFC is switching to Coca Cola starting in January. Morning Brew explains the cola wars math, the fall from first to fifth, and what a beverage menu can do for a comeback.
seoDescription: KFC is switching from Pepsi to Coca Cola after 40 years, starting in January. The market share math, the comeback logic, and the brand lesson inside.

image.alt: A red and white KFC sign with the Colonel Sanders portrait mounted on the glass front of a restaurant building
image.subject: KFC restaurant sign
image.credit: Image: KFC restaurant sign photo via SheFinds. Story source: Morning Brew, October 17, 2026

sections.heading: A 40 year pairing comes off the menu
paragraphs: KFC said this week that its US restaurants will switch from PepsiCo products to Coca Cola starting in January, ending a pairing that has lasted about 40 years. Morning Brew frames the move as a real loss for Pepsi in the long running cola wars, and as one piece of a larger comeback attempt by the chicken chain.

The history makes the split sting. Pepsi bought KFC in 1986 and owned the chain for more than a decade, then spun off its restaurant businesses, including Taco Bell and Pizza Hut, in 1997 into the company that later became Yum Brands. Pepsi kept pouring the drinks long after the ownership ended. Now the fountain belongs to the rival.

sections.heading: Why a chicken chain cares this much about soda
paragraphs: KFC US President Catherine Tan Gillespie told employees and franchisees, in a letter obtained by CNBC, that Coke products will help the chain innovate, meet changing tastes, and give customers more reasons to choose KFC. Morning Brew points to younger customers in particular, who want inventive and customizable drinks such as refreshers and dirty sodas.

The need is plain in the rankings. KFC has fallen from first in US sales in 2012 to fifth overall in 2026, according to research firm Technomic. A chain in that position does not change a 40 year supplier for novelty. It changes because every part of the menu has to pull customers back in, including the cup in the drive thru window.

sections.heading: The cola wars scoreboard right now
paragraphs: Morning Brew lays out a tough stretch for Pepsi before this news even landed:
bullets: Coke holds about 44 percent of the US carbonated soda market, compared with about 26 percent for Pepsi, per Circana
Pepsi stock is down double digits in the past year, and healthier habits plus GLP 1 drugs have hurt its North American salty snack business
Coke has recently won Culvers, Arbys, Panda Express, Marriott hotels, and the Costco food court away from Pepsi
Pepsi is not empty handed: it took Subway from Coke last year, and it will keep supplying KFC restaurants in multiple overseas markets

sections.heading: What smaller brands should steal from this story
paragraphs: The lesson is not about soda. It is about auditing the familiar parts of your offer that nobody has questioned in years. KFC treated its drink menu as a growth lever, not a tradition. Independent restaurants, venues, and creators can do the same audit on their own menus, merch tables, booking pages, and content formats.

Ask which parts of your business customers actually choose you for, and which parts are just habit left over from an older version of the brand. Then put your energy, your photos, and your video behind the parts that give people a fresh reason to come back. A comeback rarely starts with a total reinvention. It usually starts with one visible change that tells the market the brand is awake again.

title: He Turned 200 Dollars Into a 700,000 Dollar Parking Lot Business
excerpt: Brian Winch built Cleanlots by picking up litter in shopping plaza parking lots, starting with about 200 dollars in 1981. The Hustle Blower explains the property manager decision and the recurring fee engine.
seoDescription: Cleanlots grew from 200 dollars to about 700,000 dollars a year cleaning parking lots. The property manager strategy, monthly fees, and the power of saying no.

image.alt: A worker in jeans holding a broom and a green litter collection bag in an empty parking lot, with a dropped cup on the asphalt
image.subject: Parking lot litter cleanup with a broom and collection bag
image.credit: Image: Parking lot litter cleanup photo via Cleanlots. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 15, 2026

sections.heading: A childhood memory became a company
paragraphs: Brian Winch started Cleanlots in 1981 with about 200 dollars, and the family business has now lasted more than four decades. The Hustle Blower reports that he billed roughly 650,000 to 700,000 dollars a year in a 2023 interview, and described the business growing past 700,000 dollars annually in a 2026 account. Those are reported company revenue figures, not personal take home pay, and the scale took decades to build.

The idea came from his father, a janitor who took side jobs walking shopping plaza grounds early in the morning, collecting the litter people left behind. Young Brian sometimes went along and remembered two things. The work was straightforward, and someone was paying for it. After his father died unexpectedly, Brian bought basic equipment, started part time, and within about two to three months the side work was bringing in more than his shipping department day job. He quit.

sections.heading: Sell to the person whose job the problem is
paragraphs: Every tenant in a shopping plaza wants a clean parking lot, but almost none of them can hire the cleaner. That authority sits with the commercial property manager. Winch went straight to property management companies, first finding them through the Yellow Pages and asking for quotes, and the leverage is obvious once you see it.

One manager may control five, ten, or twenty properties. Win one relationship and do the work well, and a single sale can become a route of locations. The principle travels far beyond cleaning. Do not sell to everyone who notices a problem. Sell to the person whose job it is to solve it, ideally in more than one place at once.

sections.heading: The real engine is that the mess comes back
paragraphs: A car wash ends. A furniture assembly ends. A parking lot never stays clean, because people and wind bring the litter back every day. Winch clients might need service three, five, or seven days a week, so the business charges a fixed monthly fee for recurring work instead of selling each visit as a new transaction.

The customer is buying a morning arrival with no surprises, and the operator gets a calendar that does not start empty every Monday. His team added value inside the same visit too, spotting broken lighting, graffiti, dumped furniture, and damage while walking the property, then sending the manager a photo and a note. No new service line, just sharper eyes on the job already being done.

sections.heading: He grew by saying no, and Florida has the same opening
paragraphs: Clients eventually asked Winch to add landscaping and snow removal. He tried, then cut both, because they needed different equipment, schedules, and attention, and they pulled focus from the core work, even costing him at least one building. Being the best at one recurring job beat being average at five.

Florida is full of the same shape of opportunity. Plazas, venues, churches, and event spaces all need the same small jobs done again tomorrow, and the managers of those places value reliability over novelty. Pick one recurring problem, sell it to the person responsible for it in several places, report what you see while you work, and refuse the shiny extras that break the system. Boring, repeated, and paid monthly is a beautiful business model.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: His 700K secret was not picking up trash (October 15, 2026)

title: Four Yard Games Booked 9,000 Dollars as a Side Business
excerpt: Vanessa Romano spent 500 dollars on four yard games and reported more than 9,000 dollars in bookings across 65 rentals. The Hustle Blower explains why customer pickup, not the games, made the model work.
seoDescription: Four yard games bought for 500 dollars produced 65 bookings and over 9,000 dollars for Little Party Co. The pickup model and buying rule behind the numbers.

image.alt: Two wooden cornhole boards with red and blue bean bags on a green backyard lawn, with a party table and balloons behind them
image.subject: Cornhole yard games set up for a backyard party
image.credit: Image: Cornhole rental photo via Lollipop Event Rentals. Story source: The Hustle Blower, October 16, 2026

sections.heading: A 500 dollar test with a built in backup plan
paragraphs: Vanessa Romano works in corporate communications, is a mom of two, and likes her day job. The Hustle Blower tells how she still wanted a small side business, so she spent about 500 dollars on four yard games and started an event rental company called Little Party Co. The downside was capped on purpose. If nobody rented the games, her family would simply keep and use them.

People rented them. In an October 2026 interview with PEOPLE, cited by the Blower, she reported five bookings and more than 800 dollars in her first month, then 17 bookings and more than 1,800 dollars in the second. Within months she had reached 65 bookings and more than 9,000 dollars in booked revenue. The Blower is careful to note that booked revenue is not profit, and that she reinvested in more inventory as demand grew.

sections.heading: She sells an easier party, not a board game
paragraphs: The insight at the center of the business is simple. A host planning a backyard birthday does not dream about owning cornhole boards. The host wants guests entertained, without buying and storing equipment for an event that happens once a year. Renting delivers the fun for one Saturday, and then the games go back.

That framing changes what a good listing does. Customers need to know whether the games suit their guests, whether everything arrives clean and complete, and whether the set will fit in their car. Answer those questions clearly and the rental sells itself. A blurry photo and a note telling people to message for details leaves money on the table.

sections.heading: The 75 percent decision that protects the profit
paragraphs: The most useful number in the story is not the revenue. Romano told PEOPLE that roughly 75 percent of her customers pick up their rentals themselves, and only about 25 percent choose delivery. The Blower argues that this is what makes the business manageable next to a full time job and a family.

Delivery quietly eats rental businesses. Drive out, unload, set up, drive home, then repeat the whole trip when the party ends, and a modest booking turns into hours on the road. Customer pickup still needs systems, collection windows, instructions, inspection, and cleaning, but it removes the driving spiral. The most profitable feature of a rental may be how the customer gets it.

sections.heading: Buy more only when bookings ask you to
paragraphs: As orders grew, Romano reinvested, putting about 4,500 dollars in total into the business while booking roughly twice that amount. Her rule for expanding is the part to copy. She watched which games customers requested and which ones actually booked, and let that demand choose the next purchase.

That discipline matters in Florida event work too, where it is tempting to buy every lens, light, and backdrop a competitor posts. Equipment is not growth until a customer pays to use it. Start with one clear customer, one simple package of two to four games, clean photos, and pickup as the default. Let real bookings, not enthusiasm, write your shopping list.

sources.title: The Hustle Blower: Four yard games, 9K in bookings (October 16, 2026)

title: Artificial Reef Startups Want to Rebuild Florida Beaches With AI
excerpt: Coastal Assembly, an MIT startup, uses AI and marine concrete blocks to help beaches grow back, with Miami among its planned sites. The Hustle covers the Maldives proof, the money, and the other reef builders.
seoDescription: Coastal Assembly doubled a Maldives beach with AI planned reef blocks and plans Miami work. The proof, the 4.4 million dollar raise, and Kind Designs 21.5 million.

image.alt: A large textured living seawall panel hanging from chains above the water with the Miami skyline across the bay under a blue sky
image.subject: A Kind Designs living seawall panel in Miami
image.credit: Image: 3D printed living seawall courtesy of Kind Designs via Englewood Review. Story source: The Hustle, October 16, 2026

sections.heading: The beach is the product Florida cannot lose
paragraphs: Rising seas threaten far more than a nice view. The Hustle cites the scale plainly. Around 770 million people live just 16.4 feet above sea level, an estimated 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, and coastal infrastructure damage already totals about 1.8 trillion dollars, with another 1.4 trillion possible without intervention.

Florida readers do not need the global math explained. Beaches here are housing, tourism, fisheries, and identity at once. The old fixes are weak. Seawalls can be expensive and can speed erosion nearby, while dredging sand destroys habitat and washes away. A better answer would work with the ocean instead of fighting it. That is the bet a group of startups is now making.

sections.heading: How Coastal Assembly grows a beach
paragraphs: Coastal Assembly spun out of MIT, built on ten years of research at the Self Assembly Lab. As The Hustle describes it, citing Fast Company reporting, the company uses artificial intelligence to read satellite and ocean current data and predict where erosion will hit. Then it places custom blocks of marine concrete, shaped to resemble natural reefs, where the water itself can do the building.

The blocks break up waves, guide sand back toward the beach, and help keep it there, while also giving coral and marine life a place to live. Coral reefs can absorb 97 percent of shore bound wave energy, so a living structure protects in a way a plain wall cannot. Researchers keep tracking the shoreline and can adjust the structures as conditions change.

sections.heading: Proof in the Maldives, plans that include Miami
paragraphs: This is not only a pitch deck. After two years, the project doubled the depth of a beach in the Maldives. Ten more installations are planned in that area, with further work planned in the Bahamas, Miami, and Boston. The company has raised about 4.4 million dollars in venture backing, operates as a public benefit corporation, partners with the United Nations to help vulnerable communities, and earns revenue from commercial resorts.
Coastal Assembly is not alone in the water:
bullets: Kind Designs has raised 21.5 million dollars to build living seawalls and artificial reefs that protect shorelines, including work in Florida waters
Reefy, based in the Netherlands, builds artificial reefs from low carbon concrete
Louisiana startups are working on protection for low lying coastal areas, and older projects even sank subway cars as reefs along the Atlantic coast

sections.heading: Why Florida creators should watch the shoreline business
paragraphs: Coastal work is becoming a real Florida industry, with startups, resorts, cities, and researchers all needing to show progress to the public. Every installation is a story that needs filming, photography, and clear explanation, because a concrete block underwater only wins support when people above water can see what it changed.

There is a broader lesson for founders too. Coastal Assembly sells an outcome everyone can picture, a beach that grows instead of shrinking, and it proved that outcome in one place before raising money to repeat it. Start with proof in one location, measure it honestly, then scale. That sequence works for reef builders, and it works for almost every service business in Florida.

sources.title: The Hustle: The tide is high, artificial reef startups rebuilding beaches (October 16, 2026)
Fast Company: This MIT spinout designed an artificial reef to save shrinking beaches (2026)

title: Amazon Bee Wearables Record Your Day for 75 and 100 Dollars
excerpt: Amazon introduced the Bee Frontier wristband at 75 dollars and the Bee Eclipse phone attachment at 100 dollars. Morning Brew covers what the always ready note takers do, what they cost to run, and the privacy trade.
seoDescription: Amazon Bee Frontier costs 75 dollars and Bee Eclipse costs 100 dollars, recording and summarizing conversations. The features, the subscription, and the privacy trade.

image.alt: The purple Bee Frontier wristband on the left and the gold Bee Eclipse magnetic phone attachment on the right, shown on a pale green background
image.subject: Amazon Bee Frontier wristband and Bee Eclipse attachment
image.credit: Image: Illustration by Morning Brew Inc., photos by Amazon. Story source: Morning Brew, October 16, 2026

sections.heading: Two small devices with one big job
paragraphs: Amazon has introduced two new devices under the Bee name, and Morning Brew lays out the offer plainly. The Bee Frontier is a wristband priced at 75 dollars and available now. The Bee Eclipse is a magnetic smartphone attachment priced at 100 dollars and coming soon. Both exist to record and summarize your conversations so ideas, promises, and details stop slipping away.

These are the first new Bee devices since Amazon acquired the startup last year, a sign the company wants a real place in the AI gadget race rather than a side experiment. The timing, just ahead of the holiday shopping season, tells you Amazon expects ordinary buyers, not only early adopters, to consider wearing a listener.

sections.heading: What the devices actually do
paragraphs: When switched on, the devices act as note takers for real life. They transcribe what is said, summarize it, and create to do items from it. That is a genuinely useful promise for anyone whose work happens in rooms, on calls, and at events rather than at a desk.
The fuller version costs extra:
bullets: An optional subscription at 12 dollars lets users connect the devices with Amazon, Gmail, Google Calendar, Apple Health, and Microsoft Outlook
The devices carry indicator lights meant to show when they are on
Amazon says it will prompt users to ask permission before recording, and that only the user can access transcripts unless the user shares them

sections.heading: The privacy trade sits in the open
paragraphs: Morning Brew does not hide the tension. A light that nearby people might not notice is a weak form of consent, and a prompt to ask permission depends on the wearer actually asking. The Brew jokes, in effect, that wearable owners are not famous for perfect manners on this point, pointing at smart glasses as the recent example.

That tension is the whole category. The value of an always ready note taker rises with how much it hears, and so does the discomfort of everyone else in the room. Creators and event professionals should pay special attention, because our work puts us in private rooms, backstage areas, and client meetings where recording rules carry legal and trust consequences.

sections.heading: How to think about wearing one
paragraphs: Used openly, a device like this could be a real production tool. Imagine leaving a client meeting with a clean summary, a task list, and exact quotes for a proposal, without typing a note. For solo operators who are also the camera crew, the editor, and the sales team, that kind of memory help is worth money.

The rule that keeps it professional is simple. Announce it. Ask before you record, every time, and turn it off when anyone hesitates. A tool that saves you an hour of notes is not worth a reputation for recording people quietly. Amazon is selling memory. Trust is still something you have to earn in the room, in person, out loud.

title: ChatGPT Ads Can Target You by Your Prompts and Your Email List
excerpt: 404 Media bought ads inside ChatGPT to test how targeting works. The Neuron explains the two routes in, the list size rules, and why turning personalization off does less than people expect.
seoDescription: Advertisers can target ChatGPT users by prompt topics and uploaded email or phone lists, 404 Media tests show. How it works and what marketers should know.

image.alt: A Neuron illustration of a cat at a laptop while ChatGPT ads for travel, shoes, and a camera appear beside a chat, with email, phone, and prompt targeting listed
image.subject: ChatGPT ads targeting by email and prompts illustration
image.credit: Image: Illustration via The Neuron. Story source: The Neuron, October 16, 2026

sections.heading: A newsroom bought the ad to explain the ad
paragraphs: 404 Media wanted to show how ChatGPT advertising works, so it became an advertiser. The outlet ran ads inside ChatGPT with a simple privacy message, aimed at people asking about privacy and AI. The Neuron covered the test because the stunt is not the story. The targeting tools behind it are.

Reporter Joseph Cox found that advertisers can reach people in two distinct ways. One follows what a person is asking about right now. The other follows who the person is, using contact details the advertiser already holds. Together, they turn a chat window into an ad surface that feels a lot like search and social combined.

sections.heading: The two routes in
paragraphs: The first route uses context. Advertisers describe topics or keywords, and OpenAI says those hints guide matching without acting as exact match rules. Think of it as a looser version of search keyword ads, pointed at a live conversation instead of a results page.
The second route uses uploaded lists:
bullets: Advertisers can upload emails, phone numbers, or Android advertising IDs, and OpenAI matches them to ChatGPT accounts
Lists with more than 25,000 entries can be used to target people, while smaller lists can only be used to exclude people
Uploads can be raw or hashed, OpenAI says files are deleted after processing, usually within 24 hours, and advertisers cannot see which individuals matched

sections.heading: Off means less, not none
paragraphs: Users can turn off ads personalization, but 404 Media found that the setting does not stop ads or all tracking. The setting itself says ads may still be based on your current chat. In plain terms, the conversation you are having right now can still shape the ad you see, even with personalization off.

Scale is the other part of the story. Customer list targeting is standard practice across advertising, and The Neuron is careful to say so. What is new is the setting. Most of ChatGPT roughly one billion monthly users, by the estimate cited in the coverage, likely have no idea a prompt can function like a search query in an ad system.

sections.heading: What this means if you buy or sell attention
paragraphs: For marketers, a new placement is opening with unusually clear intent. A person asking a chatbot for help planning, buying, or fixing something is signaling a need in full sentences. Brands that learn this surface early, with honest offers and clean list practices, will have an edge as pricing and formats settle.

For everyone else, treat a chatbot conversation the way you treat a search box. Ask what you need, but know the topic of your chat can shape commercial messages around the answer. And if you run a business, assume your customers will soon meet your competitors inside the same chat where they ask about your category. Being the name they already trust is the defense no targeting setting can switch off.

sources.title: The Neuron: Advertisers can target ChatGPT by prompt (October 16, 2026)
404 Media: How ChatGPT targets ads to you based on your prompts, phone number, and email (October 15, 2026)

title: Meta Muse Spark Open Turns Two Mac Studios Into an AI Supercomputer
excerpt: Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open weight model with 816 billion parameters, tuned with Apple to run locally on two Mac Studios. The Rundown covers the scores, the local demos, and the open model race.
seoDescription: Meta Muse Spark Open is an 816 billion parameter open weight model that runs on two Mac Studios. The scores, the DaVinci Resolve demo, and why it matters.

image.alt: Two silver Mac Studio computers on a desk under a large monitor showing a chat window and code, with a Meta infinity loop between them
image.subject: Two Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open
image.credit: Image: Two Mac Studios via Mark Zuckerberg on X. Story source: The Rundown AI, October 16, 2026

sections.heading: A frontier sized model that lives on a desk
paragraphs: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open weight model with 816 billion parameters, built for coding and agent work. The Rundown reports that Meta worked with Apple so the model can run locally on Mac Studio hardware, which Meta presents as a first for a model in this size class.

The setup in the announcement photo is striking for anyone who edits for a living. Two M5 Ultra Mac Studios, with one terabyte of combined memory, run the model through Apple updated MLX toolkit. Meta says the same setup shipped fixes for iOS apps and edited video in DaVinci Resolve with no cloud involved. The work happened on the desk, not in a data center.

sections.heading: Where Spark Open lands in the open race
paragraphs: On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Spark Open scores 39. The Rundown notes that puts it ahead of other Western open weight models, while three Chinese models sit higher, GLM 5.3 at 45, Kimi K3 at 44, and Qwen3.8 at 40.
The pattern across tasks matters as much as the headline score:
bullets: Spark Open matches or beats open rivals on multimodal and knowledge tasks
Chinese models still lead on coding, with Kimi, GLM, and Qwen all ahead
It is the third major Western open launch this month, after Reflection AI Beam and Mistral Le Chonk, a one trillion parameter model whose weights arrive October 27

sections.heading: Meta is playing both sides again
paragraphs: Longtime readers will remember that Meta built its AI reputation on open Llama models, then moved toward closed releases as the frontier race heated up. This week shows both strategies at once. Muse Wonder competes at the closed frontier, while Spark Open gives developers and studios a serious model they can own, run, and inspect on their own hardware.

For video and creative work, local matters for practical reasons. Client footage, unreleased music, and private brand work carry real privacy weight. A model that can help edit, code tools, and run agents without sending that material to a cloud is a different kind of offer, even if a pair of top spec Mac Studios is not a casual purchase.

sections.heading: What creators should take from this launch
paragraphs: Watch the tools, not only the scores. When a model this size runs inside the machine on your desk, the next wave of editing assistants, coding helpers, and agent workflows can live inside the apps you already use, with your files staying home. That changes pricing, privacy, and speed all at once.

The open race is also a reminder to stay flexible. The best model for your work may change by the month, and the teams that win will be the ones who can swap models without rebuilding their whole process. Keep your footage organized, your prompts written down, and your workflow documented. Hardware is getting stronger. Direction is still the skill that decides what the hardware makes.
